| [THEORY-028](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-028.md) v2 | The expected bias of any data-dependent choice, and the expected generalisation error of any learning algorithm, is at most √(2σ²·I) for σ-subgaussian losses, where I is the information the output carries about the data | Russo & Zou (2015), [LIT-356](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-356.md), Prop. 1: \|E[φ_T − µ_T]\| ≤ σ√(2·I(T;φ)) for any selection T among σ-sub-Gaussian statistics. | [THEORY-031](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-031.md) | The likelihood-ratio detector is optimal under the payoff, Neyman–Pearson and posterior criteria, which differ only in its threshold, so performance is an ROC and the criterion a point on it; d′ is criterion-free only for equal-variance normal signal and noise | Peterson & Birdsall (1953), [LIT-364](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-364.md) — the threshold on ℓ = f_SN/f_N is optimal for expected value and at fixed false-alarm rate, and the two optimum families coincide (Part I Thms 1–7). | [THEORY-041](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-041.md) | Birkhoff and von Neumann proposed the modular law, not orthomodularity, and proved it fails for closed subspaces in infinite dimension; Husimi used the orthomodular identity only as an unnamed proof step | Birkhoff & von Neumann (1936), [LIT-306](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-306.md) — the lattice of closed subspaces is orthocomplemented and not distributive. | [THEORY-046](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-046.md) v2 | Expected tangible rewards for merely engaging in an interesting task lower later free-choice engagement with it | Deci, Koestner and Ryan (1999, [LIT-557](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-557.md)): across 55 experiments, expected tangible rewards given for working on an interesting task lowered free-choice engagement after the reward stopped (d = −0.40; children −0.43, college students −0.21), and lowered self-reported interest less (−0.15). | [THEORY-053](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-053.md) | A treatment's efficacy is not evidence for its theory of change: only change in the theorised process that is specific and comes before the outcome bears on it, and moving the process without moving the outcome counts against the theory | Salkovskis, Sighvatsson and Sigurdsson ([LIT-538](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-538.md)): "The effectiveness of a treatment is not evidence for the validity of the theory on which it is based", with one exception, that changing the theory's crucial factor without changing the problem disconfirms it. Hofmann and Hayes ([LIT-544](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-544.md)), from the other wing of CBT: a model whose process cannot be shown to apply "is incorrect and needs to be set aside" even if the intervention works, and a procedure that fails to move the process leaves the model untested. Active because it is close to a logical point and both state it. What it does not say is that mediation proves a mechanism; both sources deny that. | Active |
| [THEORY-066](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-066.md) | A Markov-blanket partition is defined relative to a chosen internal set, so a graph has one around almost any set of nodes, and the formalism alone does not say which set is the system | The formal core of Bruineberg et al.'s critique ([LIT-603](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-603.md), C4 in [NOTE-447](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-447.md)). In a directed acyclic graph the blanket of a node set A is its parents, children and the children's other parents, and A is conditionally independent of everything outside A and its blanket. That holds for every A, so any set whose blanket leaves something outside gets a valid internal, blanket and external partition. Having a blanket therefore picks out no set. In Friston's soup ([LIT-526](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-526.md)) the set was picked by spectral clustering with k = 8, not by the blanket. Active because it is a short derivation that anyone can check. It covers graphical (Pearl) blankets and the 2013 procedure. It does not cover the later sparse-coupling definitions at nonequilibrium steady state, which the record has not read. | Active |
| [THEORY-068](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-068.md) | In a two-alternative choice made by two competing leaky accumulators, the decision is optimal only when leak and mutual inhibition balance, so that the network integrates the difference of the evidence without loss; imbalance bounds accuracy at any fixed time and weights early or late evidence | Bogacz et al. | [THEORY-081](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-081.md) v2 | The evidence of any model formed from a full model by changing only its prior is the full evidence times the full posterior expectation of the prior ratio, so the Savage–Dickey ratio is its point-mass case and choosing which parameters to keep is evidence maximisation over the prior | Friston & Penny (2011), [LIT-620](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-620.md), Eq. 3: if models share a likelihood and differ only in priors nested inside a full prior, then p(y\|m_i) = p(y\|m_F)·E_{p(θ\|y,m_F)}[p_i(θ)/p_F(θ)]. | [THEORY-082](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-082.md) | Steepest descent is defined only relative to a metric, and Amari's proof that natural-gradient learning is Fisher efficient needs the Fisher information at the optimum to be invertible, the condition whose failure WBIC calls singular; in a multilayer perceptron it fails wherever an output weight is zero | Amari (1998), [LIT-607](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-607.md). Theorem 1 is a Lagrangian derivation: under \|dw\|² = Σg_ij dw_i dw_j the steepest-descent direction is −G⁻¹∇L, so it changes with G. Theorem 2 shows that online learning with step 1/t along the Fisher natural gradient attains the Cramér–Rao bound G⁻¹/t, and its proof uses G(w*)⁻¹. Watanabe, [LIT-616](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-616.md), Eq. 14, calls a truth regular when the optimum is one point and its Fisher is positive definite, and singular otherwise. From Amari's own Eq. 6.12, the score for hidden unit i's input weights carries the factor v_i. So the Fisher of a multilayer perceptron loses rank wherever an output weight is zero. That set is part of the optimum whenever the teacher needs fewer hidden units than the student has. Active because each step is checkable in the two texts. The claim that the Fisher is the only invariant metric is Chentsov's, cited and not held. | Active |

| [THEORY-121](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-121.md) v4 | Moral responsibility requires guidance control, moderate reasons-responsiveness of the agent's own actual-sequence mechanism, and not regulative control over alternative possibilities, so responsibility is compatible with causal determinism | Fischer and Ravizza, in their own précis ([LIT-728](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-728.md), read): moral responsibility requires guidance control, not regulative control over alternatives. | [THEORY-127](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-127.md) v4 | On the court agenda, and on any agenda in which every proposition reaches every other by conditional entailment and some minimally inconsistent triple stays consistent with two of its members negated, a group whose judgments are robustly rational under universal domain and respect unanimity cannot form its judgment on each proposition from its members' judgments on that proposition alone unless one member dictates; its judgments must supervene on the members' whole sets of judgments, and so can depart from what the members judge on the same proposition while being wholly fixed by them | List & Pettit (2006), [LIT-705](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-705.md): under universal domain, robust group rationality (complete, consistent, deductively closed group judgments for every profile of rational member judgments) is inconsistent with majoritarian, uniform proposition-wise and proposition-wise supervenience (Propositions 1–3; the last two proved elsewhere and cited), and consistent with set-wise supervenience, which the premise-based and distributed premise-based procedures achieve (Propositions 4–5). Members' judgments on a conclusion can then be insufficient, or even unnecessary, to fix the group's judgment on it. List (2014), [LIT-700](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-700.md), makes this the mark of a third kind of collective attitude: corporate attitudes, a group agent's, supervene "holistically", while aggregate and common attitudes supervene proposition by proposition. Active since 2026-10-19 for categorical judgments on the court agenda and on agendas with two stated connectedness conditions: the record re-derived Proposition 3 (and Proposition 2 as a corollary) itself. The extension to corporate attitudes in general is QUESTION-152. | Active |
| [THEORY-132](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-132.md) | Stability, a system's speed of return to equilibrium after disturbance, and resilience, its capacity to absorb change and persist within its domain of attraction, are distinct properties that can trade off, so a system can be highly unstable and highly resilient, and managing it for constancy can erode its resilience | Holling (1973), [LIT-741](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-741.md). Stability is return to equilibrium. Resilience is persistence under change, set by the extent of the domain of attraction and the system's distance from its edge. Budworm forests and insect populations in harsh climates are unstable and resilient; homogeneous lakes are stable and fragile. Active for the distinction, which has become standard. The claim that management for constancy erodes resilience rests on suggestive cases. | Active |
| [THEORY-134](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-134.md) | Whether a system can persist is a question about a constraint set fixed independently of its dynamics: a set is viable when from each of its states some evolution can stay in it, and when it is not, its viability kernel is the largest part that is, from the rest of which every evolution leaves in finite time | Aubin's viability theory, read in his 1999 mini-course notes [LIT-714](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-714.md). Given dynamics and a set K of required states, K is viable if some evolution from each state stays in K and invariant if every one does. Nagumo's theorem reduces viability to a tangency condition. The viability kernel is the largest viable subset of K; from outside it every evolution exits K. The notes do not compare viability with stability; that contrast is a further step. | Active |
| [THEORY-136](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-136.md) v2 | A persistent or abrupt change is not evidence that a system has alternative stable states: field patterns such as jumps, multimodality and dual relationships also arise from a stepwise driver or a simple threshold, and only hysteresis, initial-state dependence or a lasting shift after a temporary disturbance, with slow return excluded, comes close to showing one | Scheffer & Carpenter (2003), [LIT-726](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-726.md). Alternative attractors predict sudden shifts, multimodal states and dual responses to a driver, and so do discontinuous drivers and threshold responses. Discriminating evidence is experimental: different starting states reaching different end states, temporary disturbances causing lasting shifts, or hysteresis. Slow recovery can mimic all three. Positive feedback must be strong to produce alternative states. Active as a methodological standard. | Active |
| [THEORY-138](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-138.md) | X is a cause of Y exactly when some intervention on X with respect to Y would change Y, where an intervention is an exogenous causal process that alone sets X (M1), affects Y only through X (M2), is not caused by anything that affects Y by another route (M3), and leaves Y's causes off the path through X unchanged (M4); so defined, causation is not reduced to non-causal facts but is not viciously circular, and needs no human agent | Woodward, "Causation and Manipulability" (SEP, 2001; revised 2023), [LIT-713](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-713.md). A cause is what changes the effect under a surgical, exogenous intervention, defined relative to the effect by M1–M4. The account separates total from direct causes by combining interventions, and treats natural experiments as interventions. Active as the standard the record uses for what a causal claim asserts. This statement says nothing about invariance, proportionality or levels. | Active |
| [THEORY-149](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-149.md) | Users can govern a shared resource durably without either privatisation or central control, and the institutions that last are marked not by particular rules but by structural regularities: user-made and user-monitored rules, graduated sanctions, cheap local conflict resolution, recognised rights to self-organise, and nested layers of governance | Ostrom's account, read in her Nobel lecture ([LIT-719](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-719.md)). Coded case meta-analyses, laboratory and field experiments and multi-country field studies agree that resource users often self-govern successfully. Long-surviving institutions share eight design principles that failed ones lack. The principles are correlates of survival, not tested causes, and their reach beyond common-pool resources is not shown. | Active |
| [THEORY-155](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-155.md) v2 | Iterated learning by Bayesian agents who sample from the posterior converges, in an ergodic chain, to the shared prior | Griffiths & Kalish (2007), [LIT-769](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-769.md), read in [NOTE-599](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-599.md): a chain of learners who share a prior and each sample a hypothesis from their posterior is a Gibbs sampler, so the probability a learner holds a hypothesis converges to its prior probability, whatever the amount of data passed on; with MAP learners the outcome centres on the prior's mode but depends on data amount and noise, and can amplify weak biases. It is a theorem about an idealized chain. It does not say human chains reach the prior, and Kirby, Cornish & Smith's laboratory chains, [LIT-771](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-771.md), are consistent with it without testing it. Whether human chains do is [QUESTION-137](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-137.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-158](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-158.md) v2 | For a Markov process on a finite state space, an observable commutes with the generator exactly when its mean and variance are both conserved in every state, which is exactly when it is constant on each connected component of the transition graph, so a conserved mean alone does not give a symmetry | Baez & Fong (2013), [LIT-773](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-773.md), read in [NOTE-598](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-598.md): Theorem 1 (finite state space, four equivalent conditions), which the record re-derived. Theorems 2–3 (σ-finite measure spaces, without the component form) are reported as the source's (QUESTION-144). Unlike quantum mechanics, where a mean conserved in every state already implies commutation, a Markov process can conserve the mean of an observable it does not commute with. The theorem covers diagonal observables only; it says nothing about symmetries that permute states. | Active |
| [THEORY-160](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-160.md) v2 | In the algebraic Hamiltonian setting, symmetry and conservation correspond because the bracket is antisymmetric, which for a bilinear bracket is each observable conserving itself; the theorem's content lies in identifying observables with generators | Baez (2020), [LIT-819](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-819.md), read in [NOTE-630](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-630.md), Theorems 3, 4, 8 and 10, with Alfsen and Shultz's theorem quoted as Theorem 12 and not checked here (QUESTION-142). With unique solutions to the flow equations, "a generates symmetries of b iff b generates symmetries of a" is {a, b} = 0 ⇔ {b, a} = 0. It assumes reversible one-parameter groups and an observable–generator map; it says nothing about dissipative or stochastic dynamics, nor about the Lagrangian form of Noether's theorem. | Active |
| [THEORY-161](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-161.md) v2 | In Zhao et al.'s (2025) and Chai et al.'s (2023) semantic rate–distortion frameworks, meaning is a latent variable with a known joint law with the observation, so their limits are indirect source-coding limits; Zhao et al.'s posterior-matching semantic distortion is, with KL divergence, exactly the information bottleneck, and with total variation a bound on the expected lost value of every bounded-loss decision | From the readings of Zhao et al. (2025), [LIT-793](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-793.md), Chai et al. (2023), [LIT-812](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-812.md), and the survey of Xin, Fan and Letaief (2024), [LIT-823](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-823.md). These frameworks fix meaning as a hidden S with a known p(S, X); their theorems are indirect rate–distortion results that do not depend on what S is. Zhao et al.'s posterior distortion reduces, for KL, to I(S;X) − I(S;Y), making the function the information bottleneck ([LIT-338](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-338.md)), and for TV bounds the extra Bayes risk of every bounded loss. The two identities are this record's derivations, not the papers'. | Active |
| [THEORY-165](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-165.md) v2 | Within a fixed measurement scenario, the non-contextual fraction is the value of a linear programme whose constraint vector is the empirical model's probability table, and the contextual fraction is convex under mixing | From Abramsky, Barbosa & Mansfield (2017), [LIT-265](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-265.md): the non-contextual fraction is the value of a linear programme whose constraint vector is the empirical model (Eq. 3), and convexity of CF under mixing is their Theorem 2. Piecewise linearity and the Lipschitz bound are the record's own derivation, now CLAIM-372. The Lipschitz constant depends on the scenario and is not bounded here. Nothing here applies to signalling data, where CF is undefined. | Active |
| [THEORY-169](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-169.md) v2 | For unnormalized causal linear attention and for softmax attention, conditioning on a context is exactly training a learner on it and predicting: the first is one batch gradient step of a linear inner model from zero, the second kernel regression that stores the context, and one linear self-attention layer with constructed weights carries one gradient step of in-context linear regression; for these layers conditioning and per-sequence weight updates differ in what state is kept, not in kind | Sun et al. (2024), [LIT-801](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-801.md), Theorems 1–2, with von Oswald et al. (2022), [LIT-792](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-792.md), Proposition 1. Linear attention equals a layer whose state is a linear model's weights, updated by batch gradient descent on the context from zero; softmax attention equals a Nadaraya–Watson learner whose "training" appends the context to a list; and, with constructed weights, one linear attention layer reproduces one gradient step of a linear regression on in-context pairs. These are identities of output for specific layers. They do not say that trained transformers do gradient descent (the anthology rejects that, [ANTH-THEORY-068](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/blob/main/record/theory.d/THEORY-068.md)), nor anything about weight updates that persist across sequences. | Active |
| [THEORY-171](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-171.md) v3 | When the causal constraints on events depend on context, deterministic assignments that are causal in each context can fail to glue into one causal assignment, so causal structure is itself a source of contextuality | From Gogioso & Pinzani's trilogy: The Topology of Causality, [LIT-808](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-808.md), read in [NOTE-612](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-612.md), with the definitions of The Combinatorics of Causality, [LIT-800](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-800.md) ([NOTE-635](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-635.md)). Over a space of input histories with the lowerset topology, causal functions form a separated presheaf, and on the space Θ₃ it is not a sheaf: two causal assignments on disjoint opens give one event two outputs on their common extension. That example was checked here, and it settles the claim. The source's Theorem 2.34, that the presheaf is a sheaf exactly when no two contexts impose incompatible causal pasts on a common event, is reported as the source's. Its proof was not read, and it is QUESTION-143. It does not say any physical or quantum data display the effect. | Active |
| [THEORY-176](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-176.md) v2 | A task-loss stitching penalty compares representations in one decision problem, through a fixed top network and a restricted map class, so it is not Blackwell's order: representations that are functions of each other can stitch differently, and a negative penalty shows the fitted map did not reproduce the layers it replaced | Bansal, Nakkiran & Barak (2021), [LIT-850](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-850.md), define the stitching penalty L_ℓ(r; A) − L(A), with L_ℓ(r; A) the least task loss of A's top layers fed r through a map from a simple family S, and use it to call one representation better than another. Read against Blackwell (1953), [LIT-781](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-781.md), and [THEORY-156](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-156.md), that ordering is one coordinate of the comparison of experiments with the decision rules cut down to A's head composed with S. It is not invariant under Blackwell equivalence, which the paper intends, and it meets Blackwell's order only where the fitted map reproduces the replaced layers exactly. The relations are this record's derivations from the paper's definitions, not the paper's. | Active |
| [THEORY-177](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-177.md) v2 | In a binary cyclic system, the Contextuality-by-Default measure of signalling is twice the sum, over contents, of the least direct influence of context that a canonical causal model of the data must place on each content, and each content's least influence is the total-variation distance between its two marginals | Wang, Sadrzadeh, Abramsky & Cervantes (2021), [LIT-851](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-851.md), Proposition 1. It joins CbD's maximal couplings ([LIT-777](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-777.md), Theorem 3.3) to Jones's 2019 correspondence between couplings and canonical models, which the paper quotes and the record derives independently. The result measures signalling. Its minima are per content, each reached in its own model; one model reaches them all only if the system is noncontextual. It says nothing about contextuality beyond the bound that a rank-2 system with Δ ≥ 2 cannot be contextual, and identifies no particular causal model. | Active |
| [THEORY-178](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-178.md) v2 | In an ensemble of sign-consistent Boolean rules on the 87-gene core of E. coli's regulatory network, a transient knockout or overexpression of one gene can leave the network in a different attractor after release, and every gene that does so reaches a strongly connected component containing a positive circuit | Zhao, Wytock, Reynolds and Motter (2024), [LIT-854](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-854.md). In an ensemble of sign-consistent Boolean rules on the 87-gene core of the E. coli regulatory network, 51 genes admit a transient knockout or overexpression that moves the network to a different attractor, and every such gene reaches a strongly connected component with a positive circuit. So one genotype may hold several heritable expression states without epigenetic marks, in the model. The evidence is a model ensemble, read in full in NOTE-655, and the title claims no more. No transient perturbation has been shown to have a lasting effect in cells; that experiment is QUESTION-172. | Active |
| [THEORY-184](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-184.md) v2 | Under a permutation-equivariant update whose map is K-Lipschitz, coincident neurons stay coincident at every step size, and at step size below 1/K distinct neurons cannot merge in finitely many steps | Yang, Poggio, Chuang and Ziyin (2025), [LIT-861](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-861.md), read in [NOTE-663](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-663.md). If an update commutes with permuting neurons (GD, SGD or Adam on a permutation-symmetric loss) and its map is K-Lipschitz, one step of size η changes every pairwise neuron distance by a factor in [1 − ηK, 1 + ηK]. This is a proved constraint on trajectories. It does not say that training simplifies above 1/K, that neurons never merge in the limit, or that any scale-dependent shape of the neuron cloud is preserved. | Active |
| [THEORY-185](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-185.md) v4 | When each binary attribute of a word affects its co-occurrence independently and multiplicatively, the PMI is affine in the attributes with rank at most d + 1, so a spectral PMI embedding is a linear image of the attribute hypercube and parallelogram analogies hold exactly; over the full hypercube of words, each attribute's two values equally frequent, the raw co-occurrence ratio mixes in products of attributes, and keeps exact analogies only when the strengths are alike enough that every attribute mode outranks every product mode | Korchinski, Karkada, Bahri and Wyart (2025), [LIT-863](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-863.md): proved for a generative model of co-occurrence in which words are bundles of independent binary attributes, with robustness to noise, pruning and deleted pairs argued from eigenvalue bounds and simulated. The embeddings are eigendecompositions, not trained models; that real co-occurrence is close to this form is inferred from spectral and accuracy-curve shapes, not measured. | Active |
| [THEORY-187](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-187.md) v2 | In a deep linear network trained by gradient descent on whitened inputs from decoupled, balanced initial weights, depth slows learning through the initial end-to-end strength of each mode: counting iterations as learning time over the stable step size, from strength of order one the number of iterations stays bounded as depth grows, once the step size falls with depth as stability requires, while from small strength ε the plateau lengthens from ln(1/ε) with one hidden layer towards 1/ε at great depth | Saxe, McClelland and Ganguli (2014), [LIT-864](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-864.md), Eqs. 13–17 and Appendix B: exact for decoupled initial weights and whitened inputs, with the step size bounded by the Hessian at the optimum, and supported on MNIST from decoupled starts up to 100 layers. It does not show that random orthogonal initialisation is such a start. The paper's account of that, isometry of the product of layers, is argued and simulated, not derived. It says nothing about nonlinear networks' learning time, and it is not advice on how to initialise. | Active |
| [THEORY-191](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-191.md) v2 | In four natural odour sources (strawberry, tomato, blueberry and mouse-urine volatiles), the rank order of correlations between compound concentrations has the Betti-curve signature of points near the boundary of a three-dimensional hyperbolic ball, not of any uniform Euclidean cube tried, and human odour-descriptor profiles for 127 odorants have that of a full three-dimensional hyperbolic ball | Zhou, Smith & Sharpee (2018), [LIT-872](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-872.md): for strawberry, tomato, blueberry and mouse-urine volatiles, and for Dravnieks' perceptual ratings of 127 odorants, clique-topology Betti curves match a 3D hyperbolic model and reject uniform Euclidean cubes of every dimension tried. It does not show a tree in the data, and because the fitted odour model is a thin shell, it does not separate a hyperbolic metric from a sphere in flat space. | Active |
| [THEORY-192](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-192.md) v2 | In twelve sessions of rat dorsal CA1 from three data sets, pairwise correlations among place cells have the Betti-curve signature of points sampled uniformly from a three-dimensional hyperbolic ball, not of a low-dimensional Euclidean cube, and the fitted radius rose with the logarithm of exploration time | Zhang, Rich, Lee & Sharpee (2022), [LIT-876](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-876.md): in twelve sessions from three data sets, the rank order of CA1 spike correlations matched uniform samples from a 3D hyperbolic ball and not uniform samples from low-dimensional Euclidean cubes or shuffled data, and the ball's radius rose with log exploration time from seconds to days. It does not show that the metric, as opposed to the distribution of field scales, is hyperbolic, nor that a tree is represented. | Active |
| [THEORY-193](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-193.md) v2 | A simplicial complex grown by gluing each new d-simplex to one (d − 1)-face, by a rule that uses no geometry, has a 1-skeleton whose geodesic triangles are 2-thin at every size, so hyperbolic network geometry in Gromov's sense is an outcome of the combinatorial growth; the equal-link drawing as ideal simplices is a convention, a tiling of the hyperbolic plane for d = 2 in the manifold flavor but not a tiling of hyperbolic d-space for d ≥ 3 | Bianconi and Rahmede (2017), [LIT-867](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-867.md), read in [NOTE-678](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-678.md), for the model, the degree law and the ideal-simplex drawing. The coarse hyperbolicity of the graph is the record's: the source asserts the hyperbolic geometry through its drawing and measures nothing on the graph. Every such complex has a 1-skeleton with 2-thin geodesic triangles, whatever the flavor, so its hyperbolicity is a property of the network. The constant-curvature picture, ideal simplices in the Poincaré ball, is a choice of drawing. It tiles H² for d = 2 in the manifold flavor, and for d ≥ 3 it is not a tiling. This says nothing about whether real networks grow this way. | Active |
| [THEORY-195](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-195.md) v2 | On the Random Hierarchy Model, in the experiments reported (s = 2, L ≤ 4, small v), deep CNNs matched to the tree and trained in a feature-learning regime reach a tenth of chance error from about n_c m^L examples, polynomial in the input dimension, at the training-set size at which their hidden layers become invariant to swapping synonymous tuples; two-layer networks and the same CNNs as fixed kernels need a number proportional to the whole input space, exponential in the input dimension, and deep CNNs stay near chance when every tuple is made equally likely in every class | Cagnetta, Petrini, Tomasini, Favero and Wyart (2023), [LIT-877](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-877.md): measured for depth-(L + 1) CNNs and deep fully connected networks on the Random Hierarchy Model with s = 2 and L ≤ 4, with a large-v scaling argument for the correlation threshold and an exact one-step-gradient model of a two-layer network on one patch. The law n_c m^L is fitted, not proved for trained deep networks, and in this model the correlation threshold and the grammar's size are the same expression, so the data cannot say which of the two sets it. | Active |
| [THEORY-197](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-197.md) v4 | Mehta and Schwab's correspondence between Kadanoff's variational renormalization group and restricted Boltzmann machines is an identity of parametrizations, under which an exact RG step is a perfect fit of the data distribution; away from that point it does not make training by distribution fitting a renormalization | Mehta and Schwab (2014), [LIT-882](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-882.md), Eqs. 18–22: setting the RG kernel T = −E + H makes the RG coarse Hamiltonian equal the RBM's hidden-marginal Hamiltonian for every parameter value, and Kadanoff's exactness condition equal to zero KL divergence. Short of exactness the paper itself says the two use different variational schemes, and Koch-Janusz and Ringel ([LIT-873](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-873.md)) give a case where distribution fitting keeps the wrong variables. The free-energy part of the argument was derived independently here; Lin, Tegmark and Rolnick's v2 appendix makes it in substance (LIT-887). | Active |
| [THEORY-198](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-198.md) v2 | For a finite-range lattice Hamiltonian, a block coarse-graining that keeps all the mutual information the block shares with the system beyond a buffer makes the coarse measure factorize across the block, in 1D and, in D dimensions, when capture by a hyperplane of blocks amounts to capture by each block; barring exact cancellation of existing couplings, the renormalized Hamiltonian then gains no range, and in 1D product disorder gains no correlations across the block. The coarse-grainings actually optimized fall short of that condition, and for them the link is computed only for two-spin blocks of 1D Ising chains | Lenggenhager, Gökmen, Ringel, Huber and Koch-Janusz (2018), [LIT-881](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-881.md): proved in 1D, and in D dimensions under an extra per-block assumption and barring fine-tuned cancellations. The full-capture condition is not met in the paper's own worked case (decimation of two-spin Ising blocks keeps about half the information), and the decay of longer-range, many-spin and disorder-correlation terms as more information is kept is shown perturbatively for two-spin blocks of 1D chains only, and is monotonic only locally. | Active |
| [THEORY-205](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-205.md) v2 | For a short-range lattice model on a cylinder with a symmetric transfer matrix whose leading excited eigenvalue is non-degenerate, with block and environment as slabs L_B transfer steps apart, the uninformative information-bottleneck encoder first loses stability at β = (λ0/λ1)^(2L_B), in the direction of the boundary weak value of the leading excited eigenvector, which by the cited conformal finite-size relation is the lowest-dimension primary at large circumference; the uninformative encoder can stop being optimal at a smaller β, and nothing is shown for blocks inside a buffer shell or for the fixed-alphabet RSMI optimum | Gordon, Banerjee, Koch-Janusz and Ringel (2020), [LIT-885](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-885.md), Eqs. 3–5 and B2–C11, with one numerical check on a three-site critical Ising cylinder, reproduced exactly in [NOTE-690](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-690.md). The theorem holds for slabs of a cylinder, at the point where the uninformative encoder first loses stability. The global first transition can come earlier, and when the two coincide is QUESTION-185. The paper's "equivalence" of IB and RG relevance, and [LIT-878](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-878.md)'s use of it for RSMI filters on planar blocks, go beyond it. | Active |
| [THEORY-206](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-206.md) v2 | For networks of smooth units without biases, one hidden layer needs exactly ∏(rᵢ+1) neurons to match the monomial x₁^r₁⋯xₙ^rₙ's Taylor polynomial at the origin, and a deep network O(Σ log rᵢ), with the upper bounds holding for uniform approximation too, so the cost of flattening a polynomial grows exponentially with its degree in distinct variables and not with the number of inputs: products of many inputs separate depths, bounded-degree polynomials do not | Rolnick and Tegmark (2017), [LIT-890](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-890.md), Theorems 4.1 to 4.3, extending Lin, Tegmark and Rolnick's 2ⁿ for a product ([LIT-887](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-887.md)). Proved for Taylor matching at the origin with bias-free units; the uniform version's lower bound rests on an unproved step. The flip side, that a polynomial of degree d with c monomials costs one layer at most c·2ᵈ however many inputs it has, is the edge: the separation does not reach the low-order polynomials [LIT-887](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-887.md) calls natural. | Active |
| [THEORY-211](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-211.md) v2 | In the stochastic-differential-equation model of SGD, with a gradient-noise covariance that depends on the parameters, minibatch noise drives the difference of squared norms along a rescaling symmetry, at a rate proportional to learning rate over batch size, to the point on the symmetry orbit where the gradient-noise traces of the two parameter groups are equal, whenever both groups carry noise; so at stationarity SGD neither keeps the difference fixed, as gradient flow does, nor lets it diffuse, as isotropic noise does, and differs from gradient descent by a finite amount however small the noise | Ziyin, Li & Ueda ([LIT-1012](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1012.md), read in [NOTE-714](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-714.md)), with the gradient flow conservation law and the Itô term from Neural Mechanics ([LIT-1013](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1013.md)). If ℓ(u, w) = ℓ(λu, w/λ) for every sample, then under the SDE model of SGD d(‖u‖² − ‖w‖²)/dt = −T(uᵀC₁u − wᵀC₂w), with T = η/S. The noise has no component along the symmetry, but its dependence on the parameters produces a deterministic drift through Itô's lemma. The drift points to the noise-balanced point, and weight decay adds to its rate. In a diagonal linear network the stationary distribution follows exactly: it is non-ergodic, has a memory of initialization, and collapses to zero above a critical temperature. The law is re-derived here (2026-10-19) within the SDE model; the tests are small synthetic networks, and whether it holds in deep networks on real data is QUESTION-164. | Active |
| [THEORY-215](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-215.md) | A Hawkes process with a Lipschitz rate function and signed kernels has a unique stationary regime, which suitably started versions approach, when the Lipschitz-weighted absolute kernel mass is below one (a spectral radius below one, for a network) or when the rate is bounded | Brémaud and Massoulié (1996), [LIT-1035](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1035.md), read in [NOTE-728](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-728.md): Theorems 1, 2, 7 and 8, proved. Inhibition is allowed because the conditions use \|h\|. The conditions are sufficient, not necessary; the kernels are fixed in time; uniqueness is among solutions with finite mean intensity. | [THEORY-294](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-294.md) v2 | For a wide two-layer ReLU network with zero bias on one-dimensional data whose two classes lie on opposite sides of the origin, the tangent kernel is a constant multiple of the initialization kernel, so lazy training leaves the within-class variability of its features, NC1, where initialization put it | Kothapalli & Tirer (2024), [LIT-985](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-985.md), read in [NOTE-774](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-774.md). For one-dimensional data, two classes on opposite sides of the origin and zero bias, the ReLU tangent kernel of a wide two-layer net is a constant multiple of the NNGP kernel, so NC1 is the same (Theorem 5.1, re-derived). In higher dimensions it is measured no lower, and for ReLU higher; whether lazy training leaves NC1 in place there is [QUESTION-192](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-192.md). The inference that collapse requires feature learning is the reading's, not proved. | Active |
| [THEORY-295](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-295.md) v2 | In a community whose consensus model is replaced whenever a single sound pairwise model comparison favours the challenger, which models get proposed can hold the consensus on a false model while results reproduce almost perfectly, so reproducibility need not track convergence to truth | Devezer, Nardin, Baumgaertner and Buzbas (2019), [LIT-988](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-988.md), read in full in [NOTE-792](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-792.md). In a Markov-chain and agent-based model where each step tests one proposed linear model against the consensus by AIC or SC, replication cannot change the transition matrix. A boundary-testing population reproduces almost perfectly while rarely holding the true model, and correlations between reproducibility and truth depend on the strategy mix. The consensus is memoryless, scientists hold no beliefs, and an equal strategy mix is shown only never to be the worst, not best. | Active |
| [THEORY-297](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-297.md) v2 | A bijection between shapes is equivalent, up to null sets, to the linear operator it induces on functions; in orthonormal bases a volume-preserving bijection's matrix is orthogonal, and an isometry's commutes with the Laplace–Beltrami operator, so it maps each eigenspace to the matching eigenspace | Ovsjanikov, Ben-Chen, Solomon, Butscher & Guibas (2012), [LIT-993](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-993.md), Remarks 4.1–4.3, Theorem 5.1 with App. A, and §5.1, read in [NOTE-822](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-822.md). Orthogonality was checked; commutation with the Laplacian is cited as well known. All of it assumes a bijection. The operator runs between two different spaces, but the paper gives no structure for a non-invertible or one-way map, and the stability of truncated eigenspaces is cited to Kato, not shown. | Active |
| [THEORY-299](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-299.md) v2 | Structured and translational knowledge-graph embeddings are 0-cochains of a cellular sheaf of vector spaces pulled back from the schema, each triple scored by a norm of the coboundary on its edge and, in the squared-Euclidean form, the whole graph by the sheaf Laplacian; since the zero cochain is always a global section, what they learn is a contrastive margin, not the existence of a section | Gebhart, Hansen and Schrater (2021; AISTATS 2023), [LIT-232](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-232.md), §4 and Appendices A and C, read in [NOTE-843](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-843.md). A direct identification, covering Structured Embedding, the Unstructured Model, TransE, TransR and RotatE and not bilinear models. That existence of a section is trivial here, and that the only gluing question is whether fixed data extend, is the paper's own remark taken further by the record; it is what separates this use of sheaves from the contextuality line. | Active |
| [THEORY-301](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-301.md) v2 | The Procrustes distance between regularization-normalized representations and their average linear-decoding distance bound each other only through the participation ratio of the kernel difference: a small Procrustes distance forces a small decoding distance, but not conversely | Harvey, Lipshutz & Williams (2024), [LIT-257](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-257.md), Proposition 3 and App. A.1, read in [NOTE-834](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-834.md). With K_X = XG(X)⁻¹Xᵀ/M, α = Tr K_X, β = Tr K_Y and R_Δ the participation ratio of K_X − K_Y, P⁴/R_Δ ≤ E‖Xw* − Yv*‖² ≤ (2(α + β)P² − P⁴)/R_Δ for targets with E[zzᵀ] = I. The Procrustes–Bures equivalence is imported from [LIT-250](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-250.md). Kernels with orthogonal supports show the converse fails: Procrustes distance maximal, decoding distance as small as 2/r. Finite samples, linear readouts only. | Active |
| [THEORY-306](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-306.md) v2 | MSN's objective penalizes unequal cluster sizes explicitly and SwAV's enforces equal sizes, and in one study with mini-batches of two to eight ImageNet classes, SimCLR, MSN and VICReg lost 11 to 18 points of ImageNet linear accuracy while MAE and data2vec lost under one | Assran et al. (2022), [LIT-231](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-231.md), §§3–5 and Appendix C, read in [NOTE-850](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-850.md). The prior is explicit in MSN's loss (a KL to uniform over mean cluster assignments) and in SwAV's equipartition constraint. For VICReg it rests on an informal reduction of a simplified loss to K-means and on K-means's cited tendency to equal clusters, and for SimCLR on a cited equivalence, so the title claims the prior for MSN and SwAV only. The effect is shown with batches of two to eight ImageNet classes, one run per cell, not with natural long tails; the open half is QUESTION-171. | Active |
| [THEORY-308](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-308.md) v2 | The neural Donsker–Varadhan estimator of mutual information is strongly consistent as an extremum estimator over compact families of critics, and, for critics bounded by M and L-Lipschitz in their d parameters, its uniform deviation from the population bound needs a number of samples set by d, M, L and the parameter radius, not by the data dimension | Belghazi et al. (2018), [LIT-256](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-256.md), §3.3 and App. 8.2.2–8.2.3, read in [NOTE-828](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-828.md). On a compact domain with Lebesgue densities, the supremum of the Donsker–Varadhan bound over some compact network family is within any η of the mutual information, and the empirical supremum converges to the population one almost surely. Uniform deviation ε needs Õ(d log d/ε²) samples for d parameters, under bounded, Lipschitz critics. The guarantee is for the exact empirical maximizer, not for gradient training. The finite-sample estimate is not a bound (Poole et al., [LIT-246](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-246.md)), and the proof has two gaps a reading found. | Active |
| [THEORY-309](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-309.md) v2 | If contexts are defined by joint measurability alone, every nondisturbing correlation, maximally contextual ones included, is realized by trivial measurements on a one-dimensional quantum system, so Kochen–Specker contextuality needs a stronger operational notion of context | Budroni, Cabello, Gühne, Kleinmann & Larsson (2022), [LIT-263](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-263.md), §IV.B.2, Eqs. 27–28, adapting Fritz (2012), read in [NOTE-844](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-844.md). For a nonsignalling p(ab\|xy), the POVMs G^{xy}_{ab} = p(ab\|xy)𝟙 on a one-dimensional space are jointly measurable for each pair and reproduce p. So contextuality relative to joint measurability alone is trivial, and the review requires contexts of repeatable, nondisturbing measurements. Liang, Spekkens & Wiseman's sharpness parameter is the other known escape. | Active |
| [THEORY-312](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-312.md) v2 | The large-batch InfoNCE loss is the negative HSIC between representations and image identity plus a nonnegative log-mean-exp of the centred critic, so it bounds a kernel dependence loss from above | Li, Pogodin, Sutherland & Gretton (2021), [LIT-248](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-248.md), eq. 28 and Theorem B.1, read in [NOTE-830](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-830.md). On a finite dataset of N images with one-hot identity labels, the large-batch InfoNCE loss equals −HSIC(Z,Y) + E_Z log E_Z′ exp(k − μ₁) exactly. The second term is nonnegative by Jensen (the record's step), and for a bounded kernel it is at least γHSIC(Z,Z) less a second-order remainder (Theorem B.1, printed with the remainder's sign reversed). It does not say InfoNCE is HSIC, and it says nothing of the finite-batch estimator. | Active |
| [THEORY-314](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-314.md) v2 | Every minimizer of an arbitrary cost on the training outputs plus a strictly increasing function of the RKHS norm lies in the span of the kernel functions at the training points, by the reproducing property and orthogonal decomposition alone | Schölkopf, Herbrich & Smola (2001), [LIT-261](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-261.md), Theorem 1 with its proof (eqs. 18–24), read in [NOTE-836](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-836.md) and checked. No convexity of the cost and no Riesz theorem is used; the RKHS is built from the kernel, so the reproducing property holds by construction. The theorem is stated over countable kernel expansions of finite norm, assumes a minimizer exists, and does not cover costs that see f other than through its values at the training points. | Active |
| [THEORY-315](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-315.md) v2 | For a state whose four-state reflection orbit is realizable, generalized noncontextuality bounds two binary predictabilities by \|⟨X⟩\| + \|⟨Z⟩\| ≤ 1, so the form of a predictability trade-off, not its existence, can witness contextuality | Catani, Leifer, Scala, Schmid and Spekkens (2022), [LIT-980](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-980.md), read in [NOTE-825](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-825.md). Proved analytically, with a saturating model, for preparation noncontextuality and exact operational equivalence. The bound constrains a whole uncertainty relation only in a theory where every state has the orbit; the qubit's circle violates it, and a classical theory without the symmetry escapes it. It needs no perfectly distinguishable states, and it is not a sheaf or Kochen–Specker criterion. | Active |
| [THEORY-318](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-318.md) v2 | A bound k on the max-information between a dataset and an analyst's chosen statistic multiplies by at most 2^k the probability that the statistic overfits that dataset, and an ε-differentially private mechanism on datasets of n points keeps k at most log₂e·εn, whatever the distribution on datasets | Dwork, Feldman, Hardt, Pitassi, Reingold & Roth (2015), [LIT-964](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-964.md), Supplementary Material only, read in [NOTE-848](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-848.md) (Skimmed: the main text was not reached). Theorem 2 and Lemma 5 are proved there and were checked: P[overfit] ≤ 2^{I∞}·max P[overfit], and ε-DP gives I∞ ≤ log₂e·εn. Thresholdout's guarantee (Theorem 11), n = O(ln(m/β)/τ²·min{B, √(B ln(m/β))/τ}), is stated with its proof elsewhere. Statistical queries on a discrete universe only, and a procedure that prevents inflation, not a correction for a search already run. | Active |
| [THEORY-319](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-319.md) v2 | When two views are redundant for a label, the predictor that infers one view from the other is within εX + 2√(εXεZ) + εZ of the Bayes predictor in mean squared error, and it is linear in the contrastive density ratio, so for a bounded label and a square-integrable ratio a linear readout of m random evaluations of the exact ratio approaches it at rate 1/m, with no symmetry between the views required | Tosh, Krishnamurthy & Hsu (2021), [LIT-251](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-251.md), read in [NOTE-841](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-841.md): Lemma 1, §2.3–2.4, Lemma 2 and Theorem 3. The label enters only through how redundant the views are about it; the representation is the density ratio p(x,z)/(p(x)p(z)), learned without labels. Population level. The error-propagation results need a uniform bound on the ratio, and the low-dimensional direct embeddings are shown to exist, not to be reached. | Active |
| [THEORY-321](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-321.md) v2 | Under repeated DeGroot averaging in a strongly connected society, the consensus converges to the truth as the society grows if and only if the largest influence weight vanishes, so network structure alone, not the members' common updating rule, decides whether the group belief is right | Golub & Jackson (2010), [LIT-999](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-999.md), Proposition 2 with Lemma 1, Corollary 1, Proposition 3 and Theorem 1, read in [NOTE-840](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-840.md) with the main proofs checked. The members are naïve, not sound: they ignore repeated information, and only the first round is Bayesian. The result is in a model with fixed weights, independent signals and n → ∞. Speed of consensus and its correctness are independent. | Active |
| [THEORY-324](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-324.md) v2 | A system adapts by trial and error to an environment whose effect on its essential variables it does not know only if a second feedback, through those variables, changes the parameters of its primary feedback; and if that feedback changes them whenever, and for as long as, an essential variable is outside its limits, every equilibrium the whole can reach is an adapted one | Ashby (1952; 2nd ed. 1960), [LIT-787](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-787.md), read in [NOTE-851](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-851.md). Necessity is deduced from the trial-and-error rule against a Black Box environment; sufficiency from the theorem that a whole is at equilibrium only where every part is. The Homeostat shows it in a four-unit linear machine. The parameter changes are blind, and the account says nothing about how long the search takes, which is the subject of [THEORY-307](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-307.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-337](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-337.md) | In the comparative-question paradigm, judging whether a quantity is higher or lower than a high or low anchor pulls the later estimate of it toward the anchor, with large effects in five preregistered experiments of 128 people each, lasting through dozens of intervening word-recognition trials | Harris et al. (2019), [LIT-1067](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1067.md), read in [NOTE-876](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-876.md), and Strack & Mussweiler (1997), [LIT-1064](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1064.md), read in [NOTE-877](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-877.md). In five preregistered experiments (N = 128 each) on temperatures and car prices, estimates after a high anchor exceeded those after a low one every time (d ≈ 0.85–1.39), with 40 to 70 word-recognition trials between the comparison and the estimate. Strack and Mussweiler's three small studies show the same effect, and that it can shrink or reverse when the knowledge used to compare does not apply to the estimate. This is the effect, not its mechanism: why the estimate moves is [THEORY-335](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-335.md)'s question and is not settled. | Active |
| [THEORY-338](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-338.md) | For a list searched from the front, where reaching the i-th item costs i, moving each found item to the front costs at most twice what any rule costs on the same sequence, including rules that know the future (four times counting its own moves), a fixed order by access frequency is within no constant factor, and paying to rearrange ahead of need never helps; for paging, no online rule beats the offline optimum by less than n/(n − n_MIN + 1), and LRU meets that bound | Sleator and Tarjan (1985), [LIT-1093](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1093.md), read in [NOTE-903](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-903.md). With no probabilistic assumption, move-to-front on a sequentially scanned list is within 2 of the best algorithm in its class on every sequence, the rival being free to rearrange as it goes and to know the whole future; a list sorted once by frequency, transpose and frequency count are not within any constant; and any algorithm can be replaced by one no more expensive that makes no paid rearrangement (Theorem 3). For paging the online price of not knowing the future is n/(n − n_MIN + 1), the size of fast memory when the memories are equal. It is one list, or one two-level memory, with uniform items: it says nothing about bins, partitions or search that is not a scan. | Active |
| [THEORY-340](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-340.md) | For answering membership in a static set of n keys with the fewest worst-case cell reads, sorted order with binary search is optimal only when the key universe exceeds a Ramsey-number threshold and table cells may hold nothing but stored keys or pointer symbols; it is beaten for small universes, and by two probes once one cell may hold an encoded value | Yao (1981), [LIT-1097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1097.md), read in [NOTE-891](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-891.md). In the setting later called the cell-probe model, where only cells read are counted and both the arrangement and the adaptive search are arbitrary, ⌈lg(n+1)⌉ probes are needed by any scheme whose cells hold only keys of the set or a fixed stock of pointer symbols, once the universe is astronomically large (Theorems 1 and 1′). One probe suffices for m ≤ 2n − 2 (Theorem 2), and with one extra cell holding any value two probes suffice for m ≥ 2^{16n²} (Theorem 3). Building the table is free, so the paper prices lookup only and says nothing about whether sorting pays for itself. | Active |
| [THEORY-341](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-341.md) | Inferring not-P from failure to prove P is a deduction only under two separate conditions: Clark shows that when every branch of the search for a proof of P ends in failure, not-P is a theorem of the completed database, and a search that does not finish licenses nothing; Reiter's closed-world assumption, adding the negation of every ground atom the database does not entail, keeps a consistent Horn database consistent and can make a disjunctive one inconsistent | Clark (1978), [LIT-1087](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1087.md), read in [NOTE-894](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-894.md), and Reiter (1978), [LIT-1088](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1088.md), read in [NOTE-899](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-899.md) from his 1977 workshop report. Clark proves negation as failure sound with respect to the completed database (the clauses read as if-and-only-if definitions, plus axioms that distinct names denote distinct things), given a finite failure tree for some selection rule; it is incomplete in general. Reiter defines the closed-world assumption by entailment, reduces closed-world query evaluation to open-world atomic queries when the assumption is consistent, and shows it consistent for Horn and definite databases but not for Pa ∨ Pb. Soundness here is relative to the completion, not to the world, and neither paper says anything about a search cut short by time. | Active |
| [THEORY-345](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-345.md) | Choosing indexes for a known mix of queries and updates, to minimize query cost plus a per-index upkeep, is NP-hard as the number of attributes and query types grows, and the tools built for it choose one stored order and a set of secondary indexes per table by searching configurations costed with the query optimizer's own estimates, optimal at best relative to those estimates, with no proved guarantee for their heuristics and no term for the one-time cost of building | Piatetsky-Shapiro (1983), [LIT-1089](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1089.md), read in [NOTE-902](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-902.md); Finkelstein, Schkolnick and Tiberio (1988), [LIT-1084](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1084.md), read in [NOTE-898](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-898.md); Chaudhuri and Narasayya (1997), [LIT-1083](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1083.md), read in [NOTE-900](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-900.md). Minimum set cover reduces to choosing single-attribute secondary indexes under a known workload with a fixed upkeep per index. DBDSGN chooses the one clustered order and the secondary indexes per table against a frequency-weighted sum of access, update and upkeep costs plus storage, read from the System R optimizer; AutoAdmin picks at most k indexes by greedy search over what-if indexes. The model is steady state over a fixed workload: it prices upkeep against per-query savings, not a one-off build or sort against later lookups, and its optimality is relative to the optimizer's estimates, never to measured execution. | Active |
| [THEORY-346](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-346.md) | When information stays in view at a known place, people consult it less and rely on memory more as the time to reach it rises, in a graded trend across added delays from 0 to 3.2 seconds, even where the memory is weak and the display perfect; in one copying task a model that prices memory and display access in time alone, with no preference for either source, fits how many items people encode per look | Gray, Sims, Fu and Schoelles (2006), [LIT-1073](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1073.md), read in [NOTE-868](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-868.md), and Gray and Fu (2004), [LIT-1058](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1058.md), read in [NOTE-864](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-864.md). Adding a click to reach on-screen show information cut how often it was checked, and checks of finished settings came from memory. Lockouts of 0 to 3,200 ms on a Blocks World pattern cut looks and raised blocks placed per look, with linear trends. An ideal performer model with ACT-R memory equations and Q-learning on time alone fits four measures. That the control system has no bias toward the world is argued, not tested against a rival model. Errors in the 2004 study differed only against a group that memorized under several other changes, and the 2006 model has no wrong retrievals, no precomputation, no reuse across trials and no staleness. | Active |
| [THEORY-347](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-347.md) | Belief bases with the same logical closure can revise to opposite conclusions on the same input, so a closed belief set does not fix its own revision; partial meet contraction of a base need not satisfy Recovery, and bases keep distinct inconsistent states apart, while a belief-set model reproduces the base difference only by attaching a different selection mechanism to the same set | Hansson's Stanford Encyclopedia survey (2006, revised 2026), [LIT-1072](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1072.md), read in [NOTE-866](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-866.md), with Alchourrón, Gärdenfors and Makinson (1985), [LIT-1050](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1050.md), read in [NOTE-874](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-874.md). Bases {p, q} and {p, p ↔ q} have one closure, yet revised by ¬p one yields q and the other ¬q: statically but not dynamically equivalent. Base contraction escapes the Recovery that AGM proves for closed theories, and many inconsistent bases exist where there is one inconsistent closed set. A base marks which beliefs are held in their own right and recomputes the rest; it is not a record of reasons, sources or defeated alternatives, and the survey gives no result that bases handle iterated revision better. | Active |
| [THEORY-348](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-348.md) | When staying in one state costs a fixed amount per request and leaving it costs a fixed one-time price, switching once the extra cost paid for staying equals that price is within 2 of the offline optimum on every request sequence, and no deterministic online rule does better; with a third option the best guaranteed ratio rises to 3 | Karlin, Manasse, Rudolph and Sleator (1988), [LIT-1096](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1096.md), read in [NOTE-893](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-893.md). A snoopy cache holding a shared block pays 1 per write to keep it current, or drops it and pays p to fetch it again on a later read. Dropping once the writes charged since the last read have cost p is strongly 2-competitive (Theorems 3.1 and 4.1); with a read- or write-through option the deterministic lower bound is 3 (Theorem 3.3). It is the first competitive analysis of a rent-or-buy decision, though the paper never uses the name, and its instance is when to stop maintaining a copy. Prices are fixed and known, the guarantee is worst case only, stale reads are forbidden rather than priced, and the authors call the practical significance "unclear". | Active |
| [THEORY-349](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-349.md) | For binary outcomes and a fixed representation of individuals, a predictor can pass every test in a bounded class without being close to nature: outcome indistinguishability to tests that see the sampled prediction is equivalent, with stated losses, to multicalibration over a closely related class of sets, a predictor meeting it exists at size polynomial in the tests' size and the tolerance whatever nature's complexity, and learning one is as hard as weak agnostic learning of the class | Dwork, Kim, Reingold, Rothblum and Yona (2021), [LIT-1068](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1068.md), read in [NOTE-885](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-885.md), and Hébert-Johnson, Kim, Reingold and Rothblum (2018), [LIT-1052](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1052.md), read in [NOTE-879](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-879.md). A predictor is outcome indistinguishable relative to a class of distinguishers when none can tell nature's outcomes from outcomes drawn from the predictor, up to ε. With no access or sample access to the predictor this is equivalent to multi-accuracy or multicalibration over closely related classes, and a predictor meeting it exists at size O(s/ε²) (O(s/α⁴γ) for multicalibration), independent of nature. Learning a multicalibrated predictor is equivalent to weak agnostic learning of the class. Adequacy here is relative to the class, the outcome and the features, and is not unique; it is not closeness to the truth, and the papers say nothing about signal detection. | Active |
| [THEORY-350](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-350.md) | Under a budget on maintenance time, a stored view's upkeep depends on which other views are stored, so upkeep is not additive and adding a view can lower it, and greedily adding the single view of best saving per unit of upkeep can be arbitrarily bad; on OR view graphs a greedy over inverted tree sets gets 1 − 1/e of the saving of an optimum given as much upkeep, using up to twice the budget, if no tree-piece of the optimum alone exceeds the budget | Gupta and Mumick (1999), [LIT-1092](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1092.md), read in [NOTE-890](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-890.md), with the proofs of the journal version (2005), [LIT-1080](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1080.md), read in [NOTE-901](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-901.md), and the superadditivity first noted by Gupta (1997), [LIT-1091](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1091.md), read in [NOTE-889](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-889.md). Minimizing query cost subject to a cap on total maintenance time, one stored view can make another cheaper to keep current, so saving per unit of upkeep is not monotone and single-view greedy fails without bound (Example 2). Grouping views into inverted tree sets restores a 1 − 1/e guarantee, proved in 2005 (Theorem 8), for OR view graphs only, bicriteria, under an assumption on the optimum, with greedy stages exponential in general. The proof does not treat the negative effective costs the paper allows. Upkeep is a budget, not a cost traded against savings, and staleness and build cost are not modelled. | Active |
| [THEORY-352](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-352.md) | A pseudorandom generator exists if and only if a one-way function exists, where both are secure against uniform adversaries and every reduction is an oracle Turing machine, as statements about ensembles indexed by n; the construction from an arbitrary one-way function is only weak-preserving, so security at one length is bought at a much greater one | Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby (1999), [LIT-1051](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1051.md), read in [NOTE-880](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-880.md), with Goldreich's Foundations of Cryptography, [LIT-1061](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1061.md), skimmed in [NOTE-863](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-863.md) from the 1995 draft. Theorem 6.2.2: "There are one-way functions iff there are pseudorandom generators." The hard direction runs one-way function → false entropy generator → pseudoentropy generator → generator, by uniform reductions, with seeds of length n^10 in the direct construction. Adversaries are algorithms; the paper has no circuit version, and that the proof carries over to non-uniform adversaries is the reading's inference, not the paper's statement. Everything is asymptotic. Goldreich states the theorem and does not prove it. | Active |
| [THEORY-353](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-353.md) | For a logically closed theory, the contractions satisfying the six basic AGM postulates are exactly the partial meet contractions, and those satisfying the two supplementary postulates as well are exactly the ones whose selection of remainders is generated by a transitive relation; the theory alone does not fix the contraction, and the results concern one change of one fixed theory | Alchourrón, Gärdenfors and Makinson (1985), [LIT-1050](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1050.md), read in [NOTE-874](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-874.md), with Hansson's survey, [LIT-1072](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1072.md), read in [NOTE-866](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-866.md). Contracting a closed theory A by x keeps what a selected set of maximal x-free subsets of A share; the six basic postulates characterize exactly these partial meet contractions (Observation 2.5), and with the two supplementary postulates exactly those selected by a transitive relation (Corollary 4.5). Revision follows by the Levi identity. A selection function or ordering must be added to A, and in the finite case distinct ones give distinct contractions. Nothing here concerns iterated change, where the selection comes from, or why a belief is held. | Active |
| [THEORY-354](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-354.md) | An observer's power to refute a predictor depends on its access to the predictor as well as on its budget: against tests that see only the sampled prediction a predictor of size O(s/ε²) always passes, but if fine-grained clique counting is hard, or BPP ≠ PSPACE, some cheap tests that may query the predictor adaptively pass only predictors about as costly as nature's own | Dwork, Kim, Reingold, Rothblum and Yona (2021), [LIT-1068](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1068.md), read in [NOTE-885](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-885.md). Against sample-access distinguishers of size s an outcome-indistinguishable predictor of size O(s/ε²) always exists. Against oracle-access distinguishers, under fine-grained hardness of clique counting or BPP ≠ PSPACE, there are natures and polynomially many cheap distinguishers such that no predictor much cheaper than nature is indistinguishable. Non-adaptive queries add little; the power comes from adaptive queries. The results are conditional and asymptotic, with upper and lower bounds in different parameterisations; they say nothing about human observers or about which access a real auditor has. | Active |
| [THEORY-356](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-356.md) | When stored views are never updated, greedily storing the view of largest marginal saving in query cost gets at least 1 − 1/e of the optimal saving on a data-cube lattice or any OR or AND view graph, against the optimum for the same number of views or for the space the greedy ends up using, which may exceed the budget by one view | Harinarayan, Rajaraman and Ullman (1996), [LIT-1094](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1094.md), read in [NOTE-895](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-895.md); Gupta (1997), [LIT-1091](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1091.md), read in [NOTE-889](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-889.md); Gupta and Mumick (2005), [LIT-1080](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1080.md), read in [NOTE-901](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-901.md). A stored answer is worth the saving on every query derivable from it, less what answers already stored save, and greedy on that marginal saving gets 1 − ((k−1)/k)^k ≥ 1 − 1/e of the best saving for k views; under a space budget the same holds against the optimum in the space the greedy actually uses (up to one view over), or 0.63 − f when no view takes more than a fraction f of the budget. The bound is on saving against storing the base view alone, not on query cost, and it holds only with no updates: once upkeep enters the objective it is proved only for AND graphs in which every view is queried more often than it is updated. | Active |
| [THEORY-357](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-357.md) | Computational indistinguishability is strictly coarser than statistical closeness: without any assumption there are ensembles on at most 2^(n/2) strings that no circuit of size 2^(n/8) tells from uniform, though none of them is efficiently samplable, and an efficiently samplable pair of this kind exists if a pseudorandom generator does, since its output covers at most 2^n of the 2^l(n) strings; all of it is about ensembles indexed by n, not single pairs of distributions | Goldreich, Foundations of Cryptography vol. 1, [LIT-1061](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1061.md), read in [NOTE-863](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-863.md) (Skimmed, 1995 draft, Chapters 1–3 in full), with Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby (1999), [LIT-1051](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1051.md), read in [NOTE-880](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-880.md). Proposition 3.3 proves by counting that some ensemble far from uniform fools every small circuit; its proof is non-constructive and the ensemble cannot be sampled efficiently. A generator's output is efficiently samplable, indistinguishable from uniform by definition, and statistically far by an image count (§3.3.1). That a samplable such pair exists only if one-way functions do is cited to Goldreich 1990, not read. The book's statistical difference has no factor ½, so it is twice total variation. | Active |
| [THEORY-358](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-358.md) | In visual search among up to about 36 well-spaced items, a target that alone carries one colour or one distinctive shape part is found in time almost independent of the number of items, while a target identified only by a combination of features its neighbours carry separately takes time that grows linearly with the number of items, about twice as fast when the target is absent, the pattern of a serial self-terminating scan, and practice did not remove it; that conjunctions rather than similarity cause it is the paper's reading, not its result | Treisman and Gelade (1980), [LIT-1082](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1082.md), read in [NOTE-897](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-897.md). With coloured letters on cards of 1 to 30 or 36 items, a blue letter or an S among brown Ts and green Xs was found at 3.8 and 2.5 ms per item, and a green T among the same distractors at 28.7 ms per item when present and 67.1 when absent, linear and in the ratio of a scan that stops at the first find; 13 sessions of practice did not change it. The paper reads the contrast as feature integration: conjunction structure, not similarity, makes search serial. That reading is contested by the similarity account of Duncan and Humphreys ([LIT-1081](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1081.md)), which the record could not obtain, and it does not follow that any item unique in one attribute pops out in a real pile. | Active |
| [THEORY-361](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-361.md) | When every object but one has full grade in exactly one of two attribute-sorted lists and the one has full grade in both, finding it under min takes at least about half the objects' worth of accesses for any algorithm that only reads the lists from the top and looks up objects already seen, and, with the tied objects in random order, about as many in expectation even for algorithms that may look up any object; a query on one attribute alone costs k accesses whatever the number of objects | Fagin, Lotem and Naor (2001; full version read as arXiv cs/0204046v1), [LIT-1115](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1115.md), read in [NOTE-924](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-924.md): Example 6.3 and Theorem 6.4, the paper's proof that no algorithm is instance optimal once lucky lookups are allowed. With 2n + 1 objects, n + 1 high in each list and only one high in both, an algorithm that cannot guess must read at least n + 1 entries before it sees the target, and on a randomized family any deterministic algorithm needs at least n + 1 accesses in expectation. The paper uses the case to bound instance optimality. That it explains linear conjunction-search slopes in human vision is the record's analogy, not the paper's claim. | Active |
| [THEORY-363](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-363.md) | For finding the top k objects under a monotone combining function from m lists each sorted by one attribute, with sorted and random accesses the only costs, the threshold algorithm is correct and on every database costs at most a constant times what any correct algorithm that makes no wild guesses costs; the constant is m + m(m−1)c_R/c_S, no deterministic algorithm does better when the function is strict, and once wild guesses are allowed no algorithm has such a guarantee on databases with ties | Fagin, Lotem and Naor (2001; full version read as arXiv cs/0204046v1), [LIT-1115](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1115.md), read in [NOTE-924](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-924.md). The threshold algorithm reads m attribute-sorted lists in parallel, looks up each new object's other grades, and stops when k seen objects score at least the combined score of the last grades read. For every monotone combining function it is instance optimal among correct algorithms that make no wild guesses (Theorem 6.1), with ratio m + m(m−1)c_R/c_S, tight for strict functions (Corollary 6.2, Theorem 9.1). It is a guarantee relative to a class of algorithms under an access-cost model. It does not say that top-k queries are cheap: the absolute cost depends on the data, and is linear in N for some conjunctive queries. | Active |
| [THEORY-364](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-364.md) | When each cached value is an interval its source guarantees to contain the current value, and a query must return an answer interval no wider than R whatever the true values, choosing the cheapest set of exact reads for a SUM is a 0/1 knapsack problem, NP-complete in general and solved by taking the narrowest intervals first when read costs are equal, and for a COUNT with a selection predicate the cheapest choice is the ⌈\|T?\| − R⌉ cheapest undecided tuples | Olston and Widom (2000), [LIT-1117](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1117.md), read in [NOTE-922](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-922.md). In TRAPP a cache holds intervals that sources keep valid by pushing a refresh whenever a value escapes, and each query names a width R its answer may have. The SUM answer is the sum of the intervals, so meeting R at least read cost is knapsack (profit = read cost, weight = width, capacity = R); COUNT under a predicate has a greedy optimum. Staleness becomes bounded imprecision, never error, and only the query-time cost of buying it down is optimized: the sources' upkeep, the choice of interval widths and any cost of imprecision are outside the model. The MIN rule's optimality proof is in an unread technical report. | Active |
| [THEORY-365](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-365.md) v2 | In one study of a stack of proximity graphs on nested random subsets of the data, each element's top layer drawn geometrically, greedy search on uniform random data in 8 dimensions needed a number of distance computations that grew no worse than logarithmically with the number of items and stayed below a single-layer navigable graph's at every size tested, and in 4 dimensions the beam width needed for a fixed recall saturated; the logarithmic bound is derived only for exact Delaunay graphs of bounded degree, which the index does not build, and on 200 million SIFT vectors the measured growth departs from it | Malkov and Yashunin (2020), [LIT-1098](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1098.md), read in [NOTE-916](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-916.md) from arXiv v4. They build an index like a skip list, with proximity graphs in place of linked lists, and argue that search costs a constant per layer over O(log N) layers. That holds if each layer is an exact Delaunay graph of bounded mean degree. HNSW does not build such graphs, and Delaunay degree grows exponentially with dimension.
