For the graphs it does build, cost no worse than logarithmic is measured on uniform random data at d = 8, a saturating beam width at d = 4, and at d = 128 (200M SIFT) the growth departs from a logarithm. A proof for the graphs HNSW builds is QUESTION-187. The paper gives no worst-case bound and no recall guarantee. Construction is argued to cost about N searches. | Active |
| [THEORY-366](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-366.md) | With a fixed number of data points and a query drawn independently of them, if the variance of the p-th power of the query-to-point distance divided by its mean tends to zero, the farthest point comes within any factor 1 + ε of the nearest with probability tending to one; independent coordinates meet this condition, while data on a low-dimensional subspace, or queries that fall inside well-separated clusters, escape it | Beyer, Goldstein, Ramakrishnan and Shaft (1999), [LIT-1099](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1099.md), read in [NOTE-917](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-917.md) from the authors' 1998 technical report. Theorem 1: for n fixed data points and an independent query, var(d^p / E[d^p]) → 0 implies P[DMAX ≤ (1+ε)DMIN] → 1 for every ε > 0. The index m is arbitrary, so dimension enters only through the workload's distance distributions. IID coordinates and several correlated or non-identical workloads satisfy the condition; a diagonal line, two latent degrees of freedom and queries inside clusters do not. The condition is sufficient, not necessary. The result concerns the ratio of distances at fixed n, and does not show that real high-dimensional data loses contrast, or that indexes fail. | Active |
| [THEORY-369](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-369.md) v2 | Under uniformly distributed, independent data and queries in the unit cube with Euclidean distance and a fixed number of points, an optimal nearest-neighbour search over any index that partitions points into blocks or convex clusters of at least two points must read a fraction of blocks that grows toward all of them as dimension rises; with a five-fold sequential advantage for scanning, estimates put the crossover at about 15–26 dimensions for rectangular and spherical bounding regions, and two tree indexes measured on 50,000 points lost to a scan beyond about 10 | Weber, Schek and Blott (1998), [LIT-1107](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1107.md), read in [NOTE-919](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-919.md). Under uniformity and independence, with the expected nearest-neighbour distance used as every query's radius and integrals evaluated by Monte Carlo, the fraction of blocks read passes the 20% line at about d = 15–20 for rectangular regions and 26 for spherical ones. A crude bound for any convex clustering puts it below 610. The often-quoted "around 10" is the measured crossover for an R*-tree and an X-tree. The VA-file, a scan of compact per-vector approximations, is the paper's alternative. Nothing is shown for data of low intrinsic dimension, and the finite-dimensional bounds are not rigorous as stated. The asymptotic statement, at fixed N and for clusters of two or more points, is proved by the record by a concentration argument. | Active |
| [THEORY-370](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-370.md) | On an n × n lattice whose nodes also get long-range links drawn with probability proportional to lattice distance to the power −r, a searcher that knows only the target's position and the links of nodes already reached delivers in expected time polylogarithmic in n only at r = 2: greedy routing then takes O((log n)²) steps, while for 0 ≤ r < 2 every such searcher needs Ω(n^((2−r)/3)) steps and for r > 2 Ω(n^((r−2)/(r−1))), even at r = 0 where short paths exist | Kleinberg (2000), [LIT-1103](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1103.md), read in [NOTE-923](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-923.md). Proved for the two-dimensional lattice: with nodes, local links and the number of long-range links fixed, changing only the exponent r of the long-range link distribution moves the expected delivery time of the best decentralized searcher from O((log n)²) at r = 2 to a power of n at every other r, including r = 0, where paths of polylogarithmic length exist. The upper bound is proved only for one local and one long-range link per node; the k-dimensional statement (r = k) is asserted, not proved; the family is inverse power laws of a distance every node can compute, so it does not show that no other link structure is navigable. | Active |
| [THEORY-371](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-371.md) | For conjunctive queries without equality or comparisons, two queries are equivalent exactly when homomorphisms run both ways between the queries read as small databases, every such query has a minimal equivalent query unique up to isomorphism obtained by deleting atoms, and evaluating one against a database is NP-complete when the query is part of the input | Chandra and Merlin (1977), [LIT-1111](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1111.md), read in [NOTE-907](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-907.md). Reading a conjunctive query as its natural model, equivalence becomes a pair of homomorphisms (Lemma 13), the minimal equivalent query is unique up to isomorphism (Theorem 12), and evaluation with the query as input is NP-complete (Theorem 7), as is deciding whether one query is a folding of another (Theorem 11). The paper states equivalence, not containment, and does not state that containment or equivalence is NP-complete; those are corollaries later work attributes to it. Nothing here reaches queries with equality, comparisons, negation or union. | Active |
| [THEORY-372](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-372.md) | For c-approximate near-neighbour search over n points in Euclidean space, space n^{1+ρu+o(1)} and query time n^{ρq+o(1)} are achievable on any data set whenever c²√ρq + (c²−1)√ρu ≥ √(2c²−1) (c√ρq + (c−1)√ρu ≥ √(2c−1) in Hamming space), and no list-of-points structure, the model of known data-independent hashing, does better on random instances; without that model the curve is matched only at query time n^{o(1)} by one or two cell probes | Andoni, Laarhoven, Razenshteyn and Waingarten (2017), [LIT-1120](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1120.md), read in [NOTE-918](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-918.md) from the arXiv full version. A data-dependent tree of spherical caps, with different thresholds for filing points and for routing queries, realizes every pair of exponents on the curve, for worst-case data, with constant success probability; the equal-threshold point is LSH. On random instances with d = ω(log n), list-of-points structures cannot beat the curve (a lower bound the paper calls conditional), and one- or two-probe cell-probe structures need n^{(c/(c−1))²−o(1)} words, the curve's space at ρq = 0. Optimality for data-dependent schemes, for more probes, and for d = Θ(log n) is not shown. The curve prices space against per-query time for one query at a time; it has no workload and no build cost beyond space. | Active |
| [THEORY-373](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-373.md) | For positive relational algebra on relations whose tuples are annotated from a commutative semiring, every query's annotated answer equals its answer over provenance polynomials N[X] in the input tuple ids, evaluated at the input annotations, so set, bag, c-table and event-table semantics all factor through the polynomials; revaluing inputs can remove output tuples but never add them, and nothing is shown for negation, difference or aggregation | Green, Karvounarakis and Tannen (2007), [LIT-1110](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1110.md), read in [NOTE-913](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-913.md). Union and projection add tags, join multiplies them; the usual RA identities hold exactly when the tags form a commutative semiring, and a map of tags commutes with every query exactly when it is a semiring homomorphism. The polynomials N[X] are the free commutative semiring, so the annotated answer in any semiring is the polynomial answer evaluated at the input annotations (Theorem 4.3). It is a sufficiency result for revisions that re-annotate existing inputs, not a minimality result, and it excludes added facts and every nonmonotone operation. | Active |
| [THEORY-378](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-378.md) | When items change as independent Poisson processes with known rates and a fixed total refresh rate is shared among them, refreshing every item equally keeps the copy at least as fresh and at most as old, averaged over time, as refreshing in proportion to change rate, for any spread of rates; the freshness-optimal share rises and then falls with change rate and gives nothing to items that change too fast for the budget | Cho and Garcia-Molina (2000), [LIT-1119](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1119.md), read in [NOTE-906](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-906.md). Freshness is the fraction of items equal to their source, age the mean time since an unseen change, both averaged over time and over equally weighted items. With fixed-interval refresh, uniform refresh is never worse than proportional on either measure, by convexity (proof in the authors' technical report). Under a fixed budget the freshness-optimal allocation starves the fastest-changing items; the age-optimal one refreshes them somewhat more. It prices staleness as an objective under a fixed budget: there are no reads, no query savings, no build cost and no cost of a stale use, so it is a staleness term and not a model trading staleness against upkeep. | Active |
| [THEORY-381](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-381.md) | In the cell-probe model, a near-neighbour structure on n random points that answers in t probes with m cells of w bits must satisfy m^t·w/n ≥ the robust expansion of the metric's neighbourhood graph at measure 1/m^t (and (mwt/n)^t ≥ its vertex expansion if deterministic), so in expanding spaces such as the hypercube fast queries need space polynomially larger than the data; the bounds are average case, approximate, and fall off exponentially in t | Panigrahy, Talwar and Wieder (2010), [LIT-1102](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1102.md), read in [NOTE-914](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-914.md) from the arXiv preprint. For graphical neighbour search, to which decision approximate near neighbour reduces, on data drawn so that neighbourhoods rarely overlap: deterministic t-probe structures satisfy (mwt/n)^t ≥ Φv and m^t·t·w/n ≥ Φv(1/m^t); randomized ones satisfy m^t·w/n ≥ Φr(1/m^t, γ/t) and (mwt⁴/n)^{2t} ≥ Φr(1/m, γ/t). On the hypercube this gives space n^{1+Ω(1/(ct))} at approximation c and n^{Ω(1/(tε²))} at 1 + ε; a one-probe structure matches on Cayley graphs; low-contention dynamic structures need update time at least Φr(τ, 1/(4t²)) over poly(t). Tight only for constant t; nothing about worst-case or structured data, workloads or build time. | Active |
| [THEORY-382](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-382.md) v2 | When a web server keeps each page fragment either cached and invalidated by updates or stored and refreshed after them, materializing trades staleness for response time, and in one synthetic simulation with fixed costs a periodic greedy that moves a capped number of fragments between the two, to keep the share of fresh fragments served above a set threshold, tracked that threshold by the authors' reading of its curves, answered faster than caching alone and recovered from overload by materializing everything; no bound on its distance from the best plan is shown | Labrinidis and Roussopoulos (2003), [LIT-1105](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1105.md), read in [NOTE-911](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-911.md). Quality of Data is the share of fresh fragments in served pages; OVIS(θ) estimates per fragment the change in response time (hits and misses against refresh load) and in QoD from switching policy, and each period greedily switches up to MAX_CHANGE fragments to spend a QoD surplus on speed or buy back a deficit. The paper asserts the greedy step is best under the cap and proves nothing; the evidence is one simulator with uniform costs and no comparison with an optimum. The reading the evidence does not support: that this is a joint cost model of build, upkeep, staleness and savings. Staleness is a user-set threshold, not a price, and switching and storage are free. | Active |
| [THEORY-384](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-384.md) | A nearest-neighbour graph built by pruning each point's links against all other points with a factor α > 1, so that from every point some link is α times closer to any other point, lets greedy search from any start reach a ((α+1)/(α−1) + ε)-approximate nearest neighbour in O(log_α(∆/((α−1)ε))) steps of cost O((4α)^d log ∆), for doubling dimension d and aspect ratio ∆; the ratio is tight and the dependence on ∆ cannot be replaced by one on n, and the build takes O(n³) time done naively | Indyk and Xu (2023), [LIT-1112](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1112.md), read in [NOTE-910](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-910.md). Proved for DiskANN's "slow preprocessing" build, not the build DiskANN implements. The guarantee rests on one property of the graph (α-shortcut reachability, α > 1), gives a constant approximation, not exact search, is logarithmic in the aspect ratio ∆, which can exceed n by far, and has a per-step cost exponential in the doubling dimension. HNSW and NSG prune with α = 1 and are not covered. | Active |
| [THEORY-386](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-386.md) | When a cached interval of width W is kept valid by its source, which pushes a refresh at cost C_vr whenever the value leaves it, and queries fetch the exact value at cost C_qr whenever it is too wide, and the chances of the two per step go as 1/W² and as W, the expected refresh cost is least at W* = (ρK₁/K₂)^(1/3) with ρ = 2C_vr/C_qr, where ρ times the chance of a pushed refresh equals the chance of a fetch | Olston, Loo and Widom (2001), [LIT-1109](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1109.md), read in [NOTE-912](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-912.md). The cost rate Ω(W) = C_vr·K₁/W² + C_qr·K₂·W is least where ρ·P_vr = P_qr. The minimum is calculus on assumed forms. P_qr ∝ W follows exactly from uniform precision demands; P_vr ∝ 1/W² comes from a Chebyshev bound on a random walk used as an estimate, and the paper's simulation of a random walk measured both proportionalities. Staleness here is priced as refresh traffic: the source guarantees validity, so a stale read is imprecise but never wrong, and there is no build cost and no cost of a wrong or imprecise answer. | Active |
| [THEORY-387](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-387.md) v2 | For positive recursive Datalog views under set semantics, deleting every derived tuple that has any derivation through a deleted base fact, then restoring each deleted tuple that still has a derivation from what remains, then adding what insertions derive, leaves exactly the tuples derivable from the new base (E − Δ⁻) ∪ Δ⁺, with no derivation counts stored; the extension to stratified negation and aggregation is asserted, not shown, and the size of the overestimate is not measured | Gupta, Mumick and Subrahmanian (1993), [LIT-1114](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1114.md), read in [NOTE-915](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-915.md). DRed runs stratum by stratum: semi-naive Δ⁻-rules compute an overestimate of deletions, δ⁺-rules put back those with a derivation in the reduced database, and Δ⁺-rules add insertions. Theorem 7.1 states the result contains t if and only if t has a derivation in (E − Δ⁻) ∪ Δ⁺; the proof is in a 1992 AT&T report the record has not seen. The paper asserts, and does not show, that DRed handles stratified negation, aggregation and rule changes, that it beats the PF algorithm by up to an order of magnitude, and that it is slower than counting on nonrecursive views. | Active |
| [THEORY-388](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-388.md) | Locality-sensitive hashing answers approximate near-neighbour queries over n points with O(n^ρ) hash evaluations in O(dn + n^{1+ρ}) space, where ρ = ln(1/p1)/ln(1/p2) is set by how much more often near pairs collide than far ones and is at most 1/(1+ε) for approximation 1+ε in Hamming space, with constant success probability per query; the paper gives upper bounds only and proves no limit on what organizing can buy | Indyk and Motwani (1998), [LIT-1106](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1106.md), read in [NOTE-905](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-905.md) from the authors' 1999 expanded version, compared with the STOC text. A hash family under which points within r1 collide with probability at least p1 and points beyond r2 with at most p2 gives n^ρ random tables, each storing every point: O(dn + n^{1+ρ}) space and O(n^ρ) hash evaluations per query, ρ = ln(1/p1)/ln(1/p2), for the decision version, which ring-cover trees connect to approximate nearest neighbour with polylog overhead. Bit sampling gives ρ ≤ 1/(1+ε) in Hamming space and, by embedding, ℓ_p for p in [1, 2]; the STOC text states 1/ε and only for ε > 1. Grid bucketing gives Õ(d) queries for n·O(1/ε)^d preprocessing. Preprocessing is counted as space. Nothing is proved about whether these exponents can be beaten. | Active |
| [THEORY-389](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-389.md) | For conjunctive queries and views without comparison predicates, a stored view can be used in an equivalent rewriting of a query exactly when the view's body maps homomorphically into the query's, a minimal rewriting needs no more literals than the query, and deciding whether a rewriting shorter than the query or one using only the views exists is NP-complete in the size of the query and view definitions; with comparisons in both, deciding whether any rewriting uses the views is Π2p-complete | Levy, Mendelzon, Sagiv and Srivastava (1995), [LIT-1100](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1100.md), read in [NOTE-909](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-909.md). Every use of a view in an equivalent rewriting comes from a containment mapping from the view into the query (Proposition 3.1); without comparisons a locally minimal complete rewriting has at most as many literals as the query (Lemma 3.5), which puts the problems in NP, and they are NP-complete (Theorems 3.7, 3.9, 3.10), with two independent sources of hardness. The results are worst case, in the size of the definitions rather than the stored data, for equivalent rewritings under set semantics only; they do not say recognizing reuse is costly in practice, and they do not cover contained (partial) rewritings. | Active |
| [THEORY-390](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-390.md) | Any distribution of n × N matrices whose norms concentrate as Johnson–Lindenstrauss proofs require gives the restricted isometry property of order k with probability at least 1 − 2e^{−c₂n} for k ≤ c₁n/log(N/k), by a union bound over (12/δ)^k net points on each of the (eN/k)^k sparse supports; this makes k log(N/k) measurements sufficient for Gaussian, ±1 and sparse three-valued matrices, and does not show they are necessary | Baraniuk, Davenport, DeVore and Wakin (2008), [LIT-1156](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1156.md), read in [NOTE-931](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-931.md) from the author-posted copy. The only assumption is the concentration inequality Pr(\|‖Φx‖² − ‖x‖²\| ≥ ε‖x‖²) ≤ 2e^{−nc₀(ε)}, met with Achlioptas's c₀(ε) = ε²/4 − ε³/6. The proof is the JL argument run over a net on every sparse support, plus a step from the net to the whole subspace. Necessity of k log(N/k) is recalled from Gelfand widths, not derived from concentration, and constants are implicit. | Active |
| [THEORY-391](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-391.md) v2 | Recovery of a k-sparse vector by ℓ₁ minimization from n random measurements in dimension N switches, as N grows with δ = n/N and ρ = k/n fixed, from near-certain success to near-certain failure across a curve ρ(δ) that, for Gaussian matrices, the authors' earlier face-counting theorems fix; in 2,948,000 optimizations at N = 200, 400 and 1600, eight non-Gaussian ensembles approached that curve in a way consistent with gaps shrinking as N^(−1/2), an exponent fitted on the same data, while at finite N the location depended on the ensemble | Donoho and Tanner (2009), [LIT-1160](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1160.md), read in [NOTE-933](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-933.md) from arXiv 0906.2530v1. The Gaussian transition is a theorem of the authors' earlier papers, restated here. The universality is an observation from 2,948,000 optimizations at N = 200, 400 and 1600: strict finite-N universality is rejected, and agreement as N → ∞ is not rejected. Sparse and Hadamard matrices sit about one transition width low at small N. The title states only what was measured. Whether the agreement is a limit theorem is QUESTION-168. | Active |
| [THEORY-392](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-392.md) v2 | Every map from an n-point subset of a metric space into Hilbert space extends to the whole space with Lipschitz constant at most K√(log n) times its own, by dimension reduction to K log n coordinates followed by Kirszbraun and the non-linear Hahn–Banach theorem; for L_p, 1 ≤ p < 2, the constant must be at least δ(Log n/Log Log n)^(1/p−1/2), so √(log n) is right up to a log log factor in the worst case | Johnson and Lindenstrauss (1984), [LIT-1153](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1153.md), read in [NOTE-930](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-930.md). Theorem 1 proves Marcus and Pisier's conjecture L(X, n) ≤ K(Log n)^(1/2) for every metric space X; Theorem 3 gives L(p, n) ≥ δ(Log n/Log Log n)^(1/p−1/2) for 1 ≤ p < 2, hence L(∞, n) ≥ δ(Log n/Log Log n)^(1/2). The √(log n) comes from the √k cost of passing between ℓ₂ᵏ and ℓ∞ᵏ, with k of order log n. Whether the upper bound is sharp the paper leaves open, and the constants are loose. | Active |
| [THEORY-393](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-393.md) | Any two families of n vectors of norm at most 1 have images in ⌊C log(2 + ε²n)/ε²⌋ dimensions whose cross inner products ⟨x_i, y_j⟩ are each within an additive ε of the originals, found by a randomized polynomial-time algorithm, which for small ε is below the log n/ε² of the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma; only cross products are kept, the new vectors' norms are not bounded, and whether one set can be embedded that small is open | Alon and Klartag (2017), [LIT-1151](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1151.md), read in [NOTE-929](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-929.md) from arXiv v4. Theorem 1.2 answers, in a bipartite form, Larsen and Nelson's question whether log n can become log(2 + ε²n) in the JL lemma. The proof is convex geometry: Khatri–Šidák bounds the Gaussian measure of a body of slabs, and a weakened low M*-estimate puts a random t-dimensional subspace close to every scaled a_i. Conjecture 2.4, the same with norms O(1), is proved only for t of order n (Theorem 2.5). It is not an embedding of one point set and says nothing about distances. | Active |
| [THEORY-394](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-394.md) | Every n-point metric space embeds in Euclidean space of O(log n) dimensions with distortion O(log n), by distances to random sets of every scale followed by Johnson–Lindenstrauss, and constant-degree expanders need distortion Ω(log n) in every ℓ_p with 1 ≤ p ≤ 2, of any dimension, so O(log n) is tight in the worst case; the constants are unspecified, the lower bound rests on Leighton and Rao's flow–cut gap, and nothing is shown for trees or for p > 2 | Linial, London and Rabinovich (1995), [LIT-1155](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1155.md), read in [NOTE-928](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-928.md) from the authors' February 1995 manuscript. Theorem 3.2(1) states Bourgain's theorem ([LIT-1161](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1161.md), unread): every n-point metric embeds in O(log n)-dimensional Euclidean space with distortion O(log n). The paper reproves the distortion with a randomized map into ℓ_p^{O(log² n)} built from distances to O(log n) random sets of each size 2ˡ, and gets the dimension from Johnson–Lindenstrauss. Proposition 4.2 shows that every embedding of a constant-degree expander into ℓ_p, 1 ≤ p ≤ 2, has distortion Ω(log n), from the expander's Ω(log n) gap between flow and cut. Together these answer Johnson and Lindenstrauss's Problem 4 in the negative, which the paper does not say. | Active |
| [THEORY-395](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-395.md) v2 | For ε between about lg^0.5001 n/√min{n, d} and 1, some n-point set in ℝ^d needs Ω(ε⁻² lg(ε²n)) dimensions under any map, linear or not, that keeps its pairwise squared distances within 1 ± ε, so a random projection with a union bound is optimal up to a constant for the worst set; nearly orthogonal sets can need fewer, and the bound says nothing about typical data | Larsen and Nelson (2017), [LIT-1154](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1154.md), read in [NOTE-925](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-925.md) from arXiv v2. Theorem 2 removes the lg(1/ε) gap that Welch, Levenshtein and Alon left, for arbitrary maps. The proof is an encoding argument over a family of k-sparse vectors with k ≈ ε⁻², ending at nm = Ω(kn lg(d/k)). It is a worst-case bound by existence with an untracked constant. It is not a phase transition, and the paper notes that ε-incoherent sets fit in o(ε⁻² lg n) dimensions for small enough ε. | Active |
| [THEORY-396](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-396.md) | Every Lipschitz map from an n-point metric space into any Banach space extends to any containing space with Lipschitz constant at most C log n/log log n times its own, by averaging over random partitions at every scale, and every n-point subset of L₂ extends into any Banach space at C√(log n) after Johnson–Lindenstrauss dimension reduction; for maps into Hilbert space this is no improvement on K√(log n), and whether √(log n) suffices for every target is left open | Lee and Naor (2005), [LIT-1152](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1152.md), read in [NOTE-927](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-927.md) from the authors' January 2004 preprint. Theorem 1.10 (Theorem 5.1(4)): ae(X) ≤ C log n/log log n for every n-point metric space X, bounding the extension constant over every superspace and every Banach target at once, improving Johnson, Lindenstrauss and Schechtman's C log n. Theorem 1.12: eₙ(L_p, Z) ≤ C(p)(log n)^{1/p} for 1 < p ≤ 2, C√(log n) at p = 2, through the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma and e(ℓ₂ᵈ, Z) ≤ C√d. For Hilbert targets Johnson and Lindenstrauss's K√(log n) ([THEORY-392](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-392.md)) stays the better bound, and the paper states as open whether O(√(log n)) holds for every metric domain and normed target. | Active |
| [THEORY-397](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-397.md) | A random linear map into k ≥ 4(ε²/2 − ε³/3)⁻¹ ln n dimensions keeps every pairwise squared distance of a fixed set of n points in ℓ₂ within 1 ± ε, because each difference vector's squared length concentrates with tails exp(−(k/2)(ε²/2 − ε³/3)) and a union bound over the pairs costs only ln n; the proofs cover a random subspace, Gaussian entries and independent zero-mean ±1 or √3·{+1, 0, −1} entries, and no matrix with nonnegative entries | Dasgupta and Gupta (2003), [LIT-1157](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1157.md), read in [NOTE-932](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-932.md), give the explicit bound for a projection onto a random subspace; Johnson and Lindenstrauss (1984), [LIT-1153](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1153.md), read in [NOTE-930](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-930.md), prove the lemma with k = [K(τ) log n] and K ≥ (10/τ)² by Lévy's isoperimetric inequality; Achlioptas, [LIT-1159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1159.md), read in [NOTE-926](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-926.md) from a 2002 draft, carries the same k₀ to independent ±1 and sparse three-valued entries. The guarantee is for a fixed finite set, on squared distances, and it rests on entries being zero-mean. It says nothing about maps that go up in dimension or are followed by a threshold. | Active |
| [THEORY-398](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-398.md) v2 | A Lipschitz map from a subset of a metric space whose points are at least ε apart and whose diameter is D extends to the whole space into Hilbert space with Lipschitz constant at most 6D/ε times its own, and, by Benyamini's argument in the same paper, into any Banach space with at most 4D/ε, with no dependence on the number of points | Johnson and Lindenstrauss (1984), [LIT-1153](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1153.md), read in [NOTE-930](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-930.md). Theorem 2 gives 6D/ε for maps into ℓ₂, through ℓ₁ and a weak form of Grothendieck's inequality; Benyamini's appendix gives 4D/ε for any Banach target, through a retraction of ℓ∞(Γ) with Lipschitz constant at most 2. The bound trades the count of points for the spread of the set. Whether either constant is best possible is not discussed. | Active |
| [THEORY-399](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-399.md) | Storing every inner product of n points of the unit ball of R^k to additive error ε takes Θ(n log n/ε²) bits once k ≥ log n/ε² and Θ(nk log(2 + log n/(ε²k))) below, for 1/n^0.49 ≤ ε ≤ 0.1, and comparing these counts across dimensions shows that some n such points cannot be mapped into fewer than Ω(min{k, log(2 + ε²n)/ε²}) dimensions with additive error ε for every ε ≥ 2/√n; this is a worst-case lower bound with unstated constants, the small-ε bit count is open for k above that dimension, and no one-family embedding that small is proved | Alon and Klartag (2017), [LIT-1151](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1151.md), read in [NOTE-929](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-929.md) from arXiv v4. Theorem 1.1 gives the bits of an additive ε-distance sketch for every k when 1/n^0.49 ≤ ε ≤ 0.1, by a volume argument above and a packing of net points against random probes below. Since an embedding is a sketch, Corollary 2.1 re-proves Larsen and Nelson's bound in that range, and Corollary 2.3, using the Gaussian correlation inequality in place of a union bound, extends it to every ε ≥ 2/√n with log(2 + ε²n) in place of log n. The dimension statements are for additive error on squared distances of points of norm at most 1; the relative form for small ε follows but is not stated. The matching upper bound for one set is open. | Active |
| [THEORY-400](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-400.md) | A metric space that admits, at every scale, random partitions into small pieces with each point padded away from piece boundaries with constant probability is absolutely Lipschitz extendable: maps from it into any Banach space extend to any containing space at O(1/padding), which gives C log λ for doubling constant λ, C r² for K_r-minor-free graph metrics, C(g+1) on genus-g surfaces and C√d from ℓ₂ᵈ; the bounds are upper bounds only, and the method needs a decomposition the domain may not have | Lee and Naor (2005), [LIT-1152](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1152.md), read in [NOTE-927](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-927.md) from the authors' January 2004 preprint. Theorem 4.1 turns (ε, δ)-padded random partitions of the domain at every scale into a C/(εδ)-gentle partition of unity, and Lemma 2.1 turns that into extensions of constant 3C/(εδ) into any Banach space; Lemma 3.8 carries the partitions from X to any superspace. Theorem 5.1 gives ae(X) ≤ C log λ(X), ≤ C r² for K_r-minor-free graph metrics, ≤ C(g+1) on surfaces of genus g, and e(ℓ₂ᵈ, Z) ≤ C√d, generalizing Johnson, Lindenstrauss and Schechtman's Cd and Matoušek's trees. No lower bound shows any of them tight. | Active |
| [THEORY-401](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-401.md) | A fair lottery on the natural numbers has a uniform, regular probability defined on every set of tickets, by normalised numerosity with values in the hyperrationals; it is fixed only up to a choice of free ultrafilter, it is hyperfinitely and not countably additive, and its standard part is ordinary asymptotic density | Wenmackers (2011), [LIT-163](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-163.md), chapter 2, read in [NOTE-139](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-139.md). P_num(A) = num(A)/α is defined on all of 𝒫(ℕ), gives each ticket 1/α > 0, and satisfies FAIR, ALL and a hypercountable form of SUM (eqs. 2.20–2.27). Proved, given the axiom of choice. It is not a free lunch: one solution per free ultrafilter, no invariance under relabelling, no countable additivity, and by the author's own admission it is empirically indistinguishable from the finitely additive real-valued solution. | Active |
| [THEORY-403](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-403.md) | The single-photon Mach–Zehnder phenomenology with balanced beamsplitters and phases 0 or π, including which-way detection, the bomb tester, delayed choice and the quantum eraser, is reproduced exactly by a local, deterministic classical field model with an epistemic restriction, so that slice of interference forces neither complementarity, nor observer-dependent reality, nor nonlocality | Catani, Leifer, Schmid & Spekkens (2021), [LIT-019](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-019.md), read in full in [NOTE-018](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-018.md). Each mode carries a binary occupation and a binary phase; an agent may know at most one of N, Φ, N⊕Φ; the beamsplitter swaps N_L with Φ_L⊕Φ_R. The model gives the quantum statistics for the phase shifter, which-way detection, the bomb tester (¼), delayed choice and the eraser. The existence proof holds for that fragment. The paper's further claim, that the model is generalized-noncontextual and so classical by its preferred criterion, is asserted, not proved, and unbalanced beamsplitters already admit a no-go. | Active |
| [THEORY-404](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-404.md) | With a common prior, a sender who commits to a signal the receiver observes can induce any distribution of posteriors whose mean is the prior, so an openly designed experiment moves a fully informed Bayesian receiver whenever the concave closure of the sender's value lies above its value at the prior; at the optimum, under the paper's tie-breaking, the receiver is certain when she takes the sender's worst action and indifferent when she takes another | Kamenica & Gentzkow (2011), [LIT-1021](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1021.md), read in [NOTE-717](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-717.md) with the proofs. Proved results (Proposition 1, Corollary 2, Propositions 4 and 5) for a single ideal Bayesian receiver, a finite state space, commitment and sender-preferred tie-breaking. A judge who knows the investigation was designed to convict convicts 60 percent of defendants when 70 percent are innocent. The paper does not analyse manipulation, does not compute the receiver's welfare and does not cite Blackwell. | Active |
| [THEORY-405](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-405.md) | Adding one classifier-free guidance term per concept to a diffusion model's unconditional noise prediction samples images that satisfy several concepts at once without retraining, and on synthetic scenes it composes object positions far better than compositional energy-based models but relations no better; the reading of the summed score as the score of a product of experts holds only for concepts conditionally independent given the image, unit weights, a conservative field and the noise-free distribution | Liu, Li, Du, Torralba & Tenenbaum (2022), [LIT-770](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-770.md), read in [NOTE-597](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-597.md). CLEVR object positions, 1/2/3 components: 86.42/59.20/31.36% against an EBM's 70.54/28.22/7.34%. Relations: 60.40/21.84/2.80% against 78.14/24.16/4.26%. FFHQ attributes are comparable to LACE. Text-model composition (GLIDE, Stable Diffusion) is shown only in figures, with attribute confusion and hybrid objects among its listed failures. The product is derived at the data distribution and applied at every noise level, which [NOTE-597](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-597.md) notes is in general not the score of the noised product. | Active |
| [THEORY-407](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-407.md) | For a log-integrable linear cocycle over an ergodic probability-preserving system, vectors grow at finitely many exponential rates along an invariant flag, and for isometries of a proper metric space with integrable displacement the linear drift is detected by a horofunction, with no curvature assumed | Filip (2017), [LIT-093](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-093.md), expository notes read in full in [NOTE-078](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-078.md). Thm 2.2.6 is the Oseledets theorem, proved without Kingman; Thm 4.3.1 is the Karlsson–Ledrappier theorem, proved completely apart from cited measurable-selection results. Both are classical and not in doubt. The notes' own renditions of two other steps are flawed: Prop. 3.4.8(iii) is mis-stated, and the §5.3 tracking proof misapplies its lemma, so the Karlsson–Margulis and Kaimanovich forms should be cited to their originals. The hypotheses are ergodic stationary sampling and N → ∞. | Active |
| [THEORY-408](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-408.md) | In a one-locus model with non-overlapping generations, random mating and weak selection, gene frequencies change as if each individual maximized its inclusive fitness, so a trait that costs its bearer spreads only if its effect on relatives exceeds 1/r times the cost; the increase of mean inclusive fitness is proved only for traits whose total effect on others is not negative | Hamilton (1964), Part I, [LIT-497](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-497.md), read in full in [NOTE-401](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-401.md). Each effect an individual causes falls partly on genes identical by descent with its own (weight r) and partly on others, which only dilute. So selection tracks inclusive fitness. The threshold is written −k > 1/r (§5), not rb > c: "more than two brothers, or four half-brothers, or eight first cousins". The maximization theorem needs non-negative total effects on others; for harming traits the change only points uphill. r is exact only for loci not under selection, and Hamilton could not bound the error (§4). | Active |
| [THEORY-417](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-417.md) | 'Personal identity' names several largely independent questions, among them who one is (characterization), what a person is, what it takes for one to persist, how many of us there are and what matters in survival; the persistence question concerns numerical identity, which 'remaining the same person' in the characterization sense presupposes, and posing it as 'a person at one time and a person at another' assumes that we are persons essentially | Olson (2002; rev. 2023), [LIT-454](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-454.md), read in [NOTE-374](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-374.md). Seven questions: characterization, personhood, persistence, evidence, population, personal ontology and what matters. The distinctions are conceptual and the record holds them as stated. They do not say which answer to any of the questions is right; the entry's own answer, animalism, is argued in other sections and is not part of this account. The self is set aside by the entry, so the map does not cover the self literature. | Active |
| [THEORY-420](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-420.md) | In trained transformers, zeroing a decile of a weight matrix's singular values does damage that falls monotonically with their size in square matrices, whose random-matrix null reaches zero, but not in rectangular ones, whose null has a positive lower edge: there the smallest decile is never the least damaging and can be among the most | Staats, Thamm & Rosenow (2024), [LIT-856](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-856.md), read in [NOTE-659](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-659.md). Freshly initialised matrices of BERT, Pythia and Llama follow the Marchenko–Pastur law; trained ones depart from it above the bulk, and, in rectangular matrices only, below it. Zeroing Llama-3 8B's smallest Down-Projection decile leaves 2.0% on GSM8K from 43.2%, worse than every decile but the largest, while the same decile of the square Attention-Output leaves 40.0%. Whether the below-bulk outliers are what carries the damage is not tested: the decile mixes them with the lower bulk, and overlap with the input's principal directions and ablation importance disagree for several matrix types. | Active |
| [THEORY-422](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-422.md) | In the standard formal models of group learning, no communication network is best for every epistemic problem: costly transmission favours minimally connected or star networks, pooling of estimates by averaging favours regular networks, and learning by trying in bandit problems can favour sparse ones, so a group's network cannot be judged until its learning problem is known | Zollman (2013), [LIT-716](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-716.md), a survey read in [NOTE-567](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-567.md). Each result it gathers is proved or simulated in its source (Bala and Goyal, Jackson and Wolinsky, DeGroot, Hegselmann and Krause, Zollman). Under their idealisations the optimal structure changes with the problem, so neither "too little communication" nor unequal centrality is by itself an epistemic pathology. It is a claim about models: utilitarian optimality only, with fairness, robustness and the route to the optimum left out. | Active |
| [THEORY-424](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-424.md) | Mutual-information measures of individuality that read a system's next state off its present one measure association, not propagation: I(S_{t+1}; S_t) can be positive when the environment alone drives the system, and conditioning on the environment does not recover the interventional quantity, which can be zero where the conditional measure is one bit | Bourrat (2024), [LIT-005](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-005.md), read in [NOTE-027](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-027.md), against Krakauer et al.'s (2020) measures. A* = I(S_{t+1}; S_t) is confounded when the environment is a common cause (his Fig. 2), and his interventional Â = I(S_{t+1}; Ŝ_t) is zero there. His claim that Â equals Krakauer's conditional A = I(S_{t+1}; S_t \| E_t) is false in general: [NOTE-027](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-027.md)'s XOR system has A = 1 bit and Â = 0. Â itself depends on an intervention distribution the paper leaves open, and neither it nor the paper's two ETI criteria is computed on any system. | Active |
| [THEORY-425](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-425.md) | A connecting path trained only on clean data keeps only the behaviour the clean data ask for: between two backdoored or error-injected image classifiers, models near the ends of such a path keep most clean accuracy and lose the attack, and a path flat in ordinary loss can carry a barrier in adversarial loss that tracks the input Hessian's top eigenvalue | Zhao, Chen, Das, Ramamurthy & Lin (2020), [LIT-668](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-668.md), read in [NOTE-530](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-530.md). A quadratic Bezier path trained on 50–2,500 clean samples between two backdoored VGG-16s on CIFAR-10 has, at t = 0.1, 88% clean accuracy and 1.1% backdoor success with 2,500 samples, and 63% and 2.5% with 50; injected weight errors fail at every point of such paths. Paths trained with the standard loss between regular and adversarially trained models are flat in standard loss with a PGD-loss barrier correlated with the input Hessian's top eigenvalue (0.71–0.88). The proposition offered for that correlation rests on an assumption that would remove the barrier. | Active |
| [THEORY-427](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-427.md) | For gradient matrices of rank at most r, the Kronecker product of the square roots of the accumulated row and column gradient second moments dominates the full-matrix AdaGrad statistic up to the factor r, so preconditioning each side of a weight matrix by a fourth root, as Shampoo does, preconditions at least as strongly as full-matrix AdaGrad and has O(√T) regret for convex Lipschitz losses | Gupta, Koren and Singer (2018), [LIT-621](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-621.md), read in [NOTE-480](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-480.md). Lemma 8 is pure matrix analysis (operator monotonicity of the geometric mean); Theorems 7 and 10 give regret √(2r) D Tr(L^{1/4}) Tr(R^{1/4}), O(√T) when the spectral norm of the gradients is at most 1. Proved, in online convex optimisation, with D uncontrolled because the implementation omits the projection. Nothing here is a result about non-convex training; the deep network curves are four runs without seeds. | Active |
| [THEORY-430](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-430.md) | A real hyperplane arrangement in ℝⁿ has (−1)ⁿχ(−1) regions and (−1)^rank χ(1) bounded regions, where χ is the characteristic polynomial of its intersection poset, so these counts depend only on which hyperplanes meet and in what dimension, not on the shapes of the regions | Stanley (2006), [LIT-355](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-355.md), lecture notes read in full in [NOTE-313](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-313.md), with Lectures 1–2 and 6 read closely. Zaslavsky's theorem (Thm 2.5) is proved twice, by a deletion–restriction recurrence and by Euler characteristic; the bounded-region half has two unanswered "[why?]" steps in the first proof and an omitted fact in the second. Faces of every dimension are counted by Möbius values (Thm 2.6). The notes never use "topes" or "covectors", and do not cite Zaslavsky's own texts. A region is fixed by its side of each hyperplane only implicitly (p. 89). | Active |
| [THEORY-431](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-431.md) | For classical systems with Markovian, microscopically reversible dynamics, the entropy production of a trajectory obeys an exact finite-time symmetry against the time-reversed process, P_F(+ω)/P_R(−ω) = e^ω, wherever ω is odd under reversal; Jarzynski's work equality and the mean second law follow as corollaries, and the symmetry constrains fluctuations, not which steady state a system selects | Crooks (1999), [LIT-522](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-522.md), read in [NOTE-413](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-413.md), with Jarzynski (1997), [LIT-517](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-517.md) ([NOTE-417](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-417.md)), and Seifert's review (2012), [LIT-523](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-523.md) ([NOTE-420](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-420.md)). The work equality ⟨e^{−βW}⟩ = e^{−βΔF} holds at any switching rate, and Crooks derives it from a trajectory-level entropy-production theorem; Seifert derives every known theorem of the kind from one master theorem. These are exact given their premises. They are not proofs of the second law, since the dynamics build irreversibility in, and they say nothing about extremum principles for steady states. Their practical reach is work fluctuations of order k_BT. | Active |
| [THEORY-435](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-435.md) | In Moral Foundations Questionnaire responses, Care and Fairness are endorsed across the political spectrum, while Loyalty, Authority and Sanctity rise toward the conservative end, in every world region sampled | Graham, Haidt et al. (2013), [LIT-499](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-499.md), read in [NOTE-396](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-396.md), reporting large internet samples in twelve world regions; and Atari et al. (2023), [LIT-500](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-500.md) ([NOTE-398](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-398.md)), with the MFQ-2 in 19 nations. The profile is robust as a description of self-report. It is a finding about what people say they weigh, mostly online, mostly English-speaking, and mostly WEIRD; and Purity, which carries the steepest gradient, fails cross-national invariance in the MFQ-2. | Active |
| [THEORY-437](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-437.md) | When each agent's feasible actions depend on the others' actions, an equilibrium exists if every action set is a contractible polyhedron, every constraint correspondence has a closed graph with non-empty compact values, payoffs and the maximum-value functions are continuous, and every best-response set is contractible; convexity is not needed | Debreu (1952), [LIT-067](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-067.md), read in full in [NOTE-037](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-037.md). The theorem (p. 888) is proved by applying the Eilenberg–Montgomery/Begle fixed-point theorem to the product of best-response correspondences. A Remark reduces the continuity of the value function to a compact graph plus continuity (lower hemicontinuity) of the constraint. It is existence only, in finite dimensions with finitely many agents and real-valued payoffs. That it contains Nash's theorem is asserted; the reduction is routine but not in the paper. | Active |
| [THEORY-439](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-439.md) | Given the same few demonstrations, temporarily updating a language model's weights on them and then conditioning beats conditioning alone, most on tasks with structural rules or distribution shift and most when the update is trained in the in-context format: for models of 1–8B parameters, examples used as context and the same examples used as a training signal are not interchangeable | Akyürek et al. (2024; ICML 2025), [LIT-796](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-796.md), read in [NOTE-637](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-637.md). On BIG-Bench Hard with Llama 3.1 8B and 10 demonstrations over five seeds, zero-shot 40.9%, in-context 50.5%, per-task LoRA test-time training then in-context 57.8%; 12 of 27 tasks gain at least 2 points, and Boolean expressions falls. Training the update on leave-one-out in-context tasks beats training on bare pairs (57.8% against 51.5%). The update is discarded after each task, so it is as transient as a context. It is two benchmarks and one model family, and which task property predicts the gain is open. | Active |
| [THEORY-441](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-441.md) | In spatially compact vacuum general relativity the Hamiltonian vanishes, so time is represented by no flow on a symplectic space and change by no functions on a space of states; this problem of time does not come from the 3+1 split, is absent from asymptotically flat general relativity, and does not show change to be illusory | Belot (2007), [LIT-122](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-122.md), read in [NOTE-118](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-118.md). A formal, not rigorous, derivation in the covariant phase-space formalism, with standard results cited. The vanishing Hamiltonian and the covariant derivation are strong; the canonical isomorphism of the reduced spaces is "presumed"; the claim that an artificially covariant theory escapes is hedged ("I think"). It is classical only. It diagnoses the problem and does not solve it. | Active |
| [THEORY-445](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-445.md) | A network built from group correlations over a discrete split group of plane symmetries, pointwise nonlinearities and coset pooling is equivariant to that group by construction, through the regular representation alone: the group is fixed before training and built into the weight sharing, not found in the data | Cohen & Welling (2016), [LIT-314](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-314.md), read in [NOTE-288](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-288.md). G-correlation commutes with the left action of G by the change of variables h → uh (eq. 12), and so do pointwise nonlinearities and pooling over cosets, up to edge effects and for rotations that are symmetries of the grid. Matched-parameter p4 and p4m layers lowered rotated-MNIST error from 5.03% to 2.28% and plain-CIFAR10 error from 9.45% to 6.46%. The paper uses no irreducible representations, characters or Fourier analysis, learns nothing about which symmetry the data have, and does not separate the effect of equivariance from the changed channel structure. | Active |
| [THEORY-450](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-450.md) | Across 1,176 premodern archaeological sites, the house-size Gini rises only weakly with the number of levels of political hierarchy and with polity population, and the spread of Gini widens with scale: scale raises the ceiling on domestic wealth inequality without setting its level | Feinman et al. (2025), [LIT-087](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-087.md), read in full with its SI in [NOTE-049](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-049.md). Bivariate fits on the GINI project's site-level file (47,019 houses): levels of hierarchy give r² 0.16 (all sites), 0.22 (apex), 0.27 (sites with 50 or more houses); log polity population gives 0.11, 0.21, 0.08. The scatters fan out as scale grows, and the sites that reach Gini above 0.75 are autocratic apices of polities with three or more levels. The negative claim, that scale does not fix inequality, is what the record believes. The positive claim, that governance decides it, rests on an expert-coded index partly read from architecture and on a composite whose higher r² comes from summing two predictors; it is not part of this account. | Active |
| [THEORY-455](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-455.md) | Every finite stochastic transition matrix on a configuration space equals the entrywise squared modulus of a complex matrix, unitary after dilation, so the Hilbert-space formalism can be written over any indivisible stochastic process as a non-unique representation; within that representation interference is the term by which the process fails to divide at an intermediate time, relative to the chosen configurations, and an ideal correlating environment restores divisibility | Barandes (2023), [LIT-086](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-086.md), read in full in [NOTE-080](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-080.md). Γ_ij = \|Θ_ij\|² = tr(Θ†P_iΘP_j) is an identity (Θ_ij = √Γ_ij works), and a unitary Θ on the original space exists only for doubly stochastic Γ. Interference is the cross-term of Eq. 43 against a would-be Markov factorization, and a perfectly correlating environment that then evolves separately makes the process divisible (Eqs. 45–56). The "emergent" Schrödinger equation is the definition of H, unitarity is a choice the claimed gauge freedom does not preserve, and the decomposition is relative to a configuration basis the paper never fixes. | Active |
| [THEORY-456](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-456.md) | Iterating Ollivier–Ricci flow on edge weights lengthens edges between communities relative to edges within them, so a weight threshold can separate the communities; but the separation is proved only on symmetric clique graphs under the uniform neighbour measure, and there only by a constant factor for gateway edges, and on a two-block stochastic block model the method fails at an inter/intra ratio near 0.55, where other methods still recover the blocks and well short of the detectability threshold near 0.78 | Ni, Lin, Luo & Gao (2019), [LIT-004](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-004.md), read in full with its SI in [NOTE-006](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-006.md), which checked Lemma E.1 by linear programming and iterated the proof's matrix. The flow w ← (1 − κ)d replaces each weight by the transport cost between the endpoints' neighbourhoods; bridge edges, with few shared neighbours, are negatively curved and grow. Theorem 4.1 (α = p = 0, cliques G(a,b), a > b ≥ 2) shows only non-gateway intra-clique edges shrinking; gateway edges grow at the inter-community rate with a ratio k ∈ (0,1) from Maple. Experiments use α = ½, p = 2, which no theorem covers. The Kesten–Stigum figure is [NOTE-006](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-006.md)'s calculation. | Active |
| [THEORY-463](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-463.md) | In classical statistical mechanics a strictly irreversible approach to equilibrium cannot come from the isolated Hamiltonian dynamics alone: the fine-grained Gibbs entropy is constant and bounded systems recur, so each account surveyed either weakens the target to typical or long-run behaviour or adds something from outside the dynamics | Frigg & Werndl (2023), [LIT-114](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-114.md), the SEP entry, read in [NOTE-103](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-103.md). The impossibility half rests on standard consequences of Liouville's theorem, time-reversal invariance and Poincaré recurrence. The classification half is the survey's: it is stated account by account, not argued as a general result. The entry is classical only, excludes the direction of time, and reports rather than settles the disputes about each repair. | Active |
| [THEORY-466](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-466.md) | Among contestants of equal prowess with dangerous weapons, individual selection can favour conventional fighting backed by retaliation: an escalating Hawk is not evolutionarily stable, Retaliator is at most neutrally stable because Mouse ties it, and in a contest settled by persistence alone no fixed persistence is stable while an exponential mixture is | Maynard Smith & Price (1973), [LIT-505](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-505.md), read in full in [NOTE-404](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-404.md). A simulation of five strategies, 2,000 contests per pairing, shows that "limited war" can be favoured by individual selection, without benefit to the species. The paper calls Retaliator an ESS "though Mouse does equally well", which fails its own second condition. There is no Hawk–Dove game, no "dove", no difference in prowess and no ownership, so it is not the source of display, deference or owner–intruder conventions. | Active |
| [THEORY-469](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-469.md) | Because persistence (mean absolute fitness at least 1) and selection (fitness differences) are logically independent, niche construction theory's evolutionary niche, read externally as the factors producing fitness differences in a population, differs in extension from the realized population ecological niche even after unit and modality are matched, so it is not a simple translation of Hutchinson's niche | Trappes (2021), [LIT-169](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-169.md), read in [NOTE-155](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-155.md). The non-identity follows from a conceptual argument the reading grades strong. The three kinds of case that populate the gap are weaker: habitat degradation rests on a projected persistence failure, commensalism on one field study after the author's first candidate failed, and non-limiting resources on a "possible example". The result is scoped to Odling-Smee, Laland & Feldman's 2003 niche concept and to the externalist reading of selection pressure. It does not say the two niches differ much; they "still coincide to a large extent". | Active |
| [THEORY-471](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-471.md) | Psychological states are not the machine-table states of an organism's unique best description as a probabilistic automaton, because some are never occurrent, several hold at once, there are indefinitely many and they contain one another, none of which a machine-table state can be; this leaves open that they are computational states of such a system | Block & Fodor (1972), [LIT-641](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-641.md), read in [NOTE-491](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-491.md). Five independent arguments against the machine-state identity theory, each with a stated escape that keeps functionalism: dispositions with no occurrent state, simultaneous states, too-fine individuation, productivity and constituent structure. They refute the machine-table clause, not functionalism. The paper's remaining argument (its third), inverted or absent qualia, is the only one aimed at functionalism broadly, and it is explicitly prima facie. | Active |
| [THEORY-472](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-472.md) v2 | A speaker who chooses words to minimise the information lost about a single intended referent, with words' literal meanings uniform over their extensions, picks each true word with probability inversely proportional to a power of its extension, so the size principle follows from informative communication; in one betting experiment, learners who knew the referent bet on a novel word's meaning in line with the inversion of that speaker (r = .93 on condition means), and in one free-description study speakers' word use followed it only weakly (r = .19) | Frank, Goodman, Lai and Tenenbaum (2009), [LIT-824](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-824.md), read in full in [NOTE-627](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-627.md). The derivation (utility −D_KL from intended to literal meaning gives P(w) ∝ \|w\|^(−α) for a point referent) is a proof under its assumptions. Learners' bets track the parameter-free inversion at r = .93 on condition means (700 web participants); speakers' tag-word use in free descriptions correlates at r = .19, .51 without colour terms and .02 for them. In these displays the informative-speaker learner and a plain size-principle learner coincide by construction, so the fit does not show that learners reason about the speaker. | Active |
| [THEORY-473](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-473.md) | Scaled down to one organism, Hutchinson's niche, defined as the conditions that give that individual an expected lifetime reproductive success of at least one, is observed only as a point; the rest of it is counterfactual, reached by translocation in only a few dimensions and otherwise inferred from other individuals, so in practice it is the niche of a phenotype class, and its authors call it mostly metaphorical | Takola & Schielzeth (2022), [LIT-127](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-127.md), read in full in [NOTE-170](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-170.md). The working definition (p. 5) gives the individualized niche an absolute-fitness boundary, expected LRS ≥ 1, and splits it into realized, potential, time-slice, prospective and trajectory-based niches. That the realized niche is a point and the potential niche unobservable follows from the definitions. The paper concedes there is "no empirical solution" at the individual level (p. 15), and its fix, marginalizing fitness functions across individuals, is schematic. It is a framework for structuring research, by its authors' own account, not a measurement. | Active |
| [THEORY-474](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-474.md) | Spekkens' toy bit theory, restricted to maximal knowledge and post-selected measurements, has a universal, sound and complete ZX-style graphical calculus whose phase-free rules and symplectic check-matrix conditions are exactly those of pure qubit stabilizer theory; the two calculi differ in the phase group, the Klein four-group against Z₄ | Backens & Duman (2014), [LIT-054](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-054.md), read in full in [NOTE-066](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-066.md). A red–green spider calculus interpreted in the category of relations is universal and sound, and complete by Backens' stabilizer route. A binary matrix is a valid toy state iff SᵀJS = 0, the stabilizer condition (Lemma 3). The phase-free rules coincide with stabilizer ZX. That the phase group is the only categorical difference is cited, not shown, and completeness leans on analogy for several steps. The paper does no ψ-epistemic analysis and says nothing about which operational difference the phase group carries. | Active |
| [THEORY-475](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-475.md) | In simulations from the drift-diffusion model itself, with 12 subjects and 20 to 150 trials each, hierarchical Bayesian estimation recovers every DDM parameter with less error than per-subject maximum likelihood, χ²-quantile fitting or non-hierarchical Bayes, most of all at few trials; whether the gain survives misspecification, and how much of the power gain is the hierarchy's, is not shown | Wiecki, Sofer & Frank (2013), [LIT-563](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-563.md), read in [NOTE-466](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-466.md). Experiment 1 gives the lowest trimmed recovery error for HB on every parameter, and HB beat ML on the same data sets in every condition. Experiments 2–3 report more power to detect drift differences and trial-wise covariate effects, but HB was judged by a posterior-interval test and the others by t-tests, and the clean comparison was omitted. All data were generated from DDMs, with sz = st = 0. It is the standard partial-pooling result shown for one model family, not a test of the DDM. | Active |
| [THEORY-477](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-477.md) | None of the ten morphosyntactic criteria linguists use to identify words is necessary and sufficient for the orthographic word across languages, and the test batteries that combine them pick criteria opportunistically, so no cross-linguistically valid definition of the word is yet available | Haspelmath (2011), [LIT-063](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-063.md), read in full in [NOTE-073](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-073.md). Each of ten criteria (pauses, free occurrence, mobility, uninterruptibility, non-selectivity, non-coordinatability, anaphoric islandhood, nonextractability, morphophonological idiosyncrasy, biuniqueness) fails as necessary and sufficient against cross-linguistic counterexamples, and nine published batteries use no common set (Table 1). The target is orthographic practice by design. It does not say that words cannot be defined within one language, that sub-word units are privileged, or that morphology and syntax are shown to be one domain; whether units cluster on a boundness scale is open. | Active |
| [THEORY-478](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-478.md) v2 | If the diffusion densities' Hellinger distances obey a Hölder bound with exponent θ in d_T / t^(1/β) and are bounded below once d_T exceeds a multiple of t^(1/β), then for 0 < α < θ/β summing scale-weighted hyperbolic distances between diffusion densities over dyadic times gives a distance two-sided equivalent, up to constants, to min{1, d_T^(αβ)} for pairs above the finest scale: it keeps the tree's neighbourhoods and not its global distances; whether a tree's heat kernel, or sampled data, meets the bounds, and with which θ, is not shown | Lin, Coifman, Mishne & Talmon (2023), [LIT-870](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-870.md), read in [NOTE-675](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-675.md). The hyperbolic diffusion distance is equivalent to min{1, d_T^(2α)} for 0 < α < 1/2 (Proposition C.4), under heat-kernel bounds on the tree that are cited rather than proved; one Hölder step holds only for d_T ≥ 1, and repaired, the reader finds the admissible range halves. Pairs beyond a radius are only known to be far, which matches the method's best mean average precision and its higher distortion than hyperbolic MDS on five graph benchmarks. A Euclidean distance on the same multiscale features does far worse. | Active |
| [THEORY-479](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-479.md) | Shannon's chain rule is the 1-cocycle equation of a cohomology of finite probability spaces whose action is averaged conditioning, and on connected, sufficiently rich structures of partitions every measurable 1-cocycle is a constant multiple of Shannon entropy, with no symmetry or continuity axiom assumed; in the unitary-invariant quantum version the first cohomology vanishes and von Neumann entropy is the 0-cochain whose coboundary is minus Shannon entropy | Baudot & Bennequin (2015), [LIT-053](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-053.md), read in [NOTE-088](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-088.md). Theorems 1 and 3 are proved for finite spaces, through the Tverberg–Kendall–Lee result on measurable solutions of the fundamental equation of information. The hypotheses are stated three different ways in the paper; Theorem 1's is operative. The higher mutual informations appear as coboundaries, and Theorems B, D and F and the synergy reading are sketched or deferred to companion papers, so they are not part of this account. | Active |
| [THEORY-482](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-482.md) | For a closed quantum system that starts thermal and is measured projectively in energy before and after a unitary drive, the two-point-measurement work obeys the Jarzynski equality and the Tasaki–Crooks relation in exactly the classical form, because those energy measurements erase the coherences in which a quantum difference could appear | Vinjanampathy & Anders (2015/16), [LIT-010](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-010.md), read in full in [NOTE-011](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-011.md), which reproduces the derivation (Eqs. 24–30). With W_{m,n} = E_m^(τ) − E_n^(0), a thermal start and closed unitary evolution, ⟨e^{−βW}⟩ = e^{−βΔF} follows from Σ_n p_{m\|n} = 1 (Eq. 29), identical in form to the classical relation. The identity is exact under its conditions. Its classicality is bought by the definition of work: two projective energy measurements destroy coherences, which is why the definition is contested. It says nothing about work defined without them. | Active |
| [THEORY-489](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-489.md) | Chains of human function learners, each trained on the previous learner's responses, forget their starting function and in 28 of 32 families converge within a few generations to a positive linear function, the bias earlier studies report, whatever function trained the first learner; this is convergence to the learners' favoured function, not shown to be convergence to their prior | Kalish, Griffiths & Lewandowsky (2007), [LIT-820](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-820.md), read in [NOTE-616](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-616.md). 288 participants in 32 nine-generation chains, four starting conditions. 28 families converged to a positive linear function; 3 converged to the negative linear one and 1 had not converged. The bias was taken from earlier studies, not measured on these learners, and stationarity was not established. It supports the claim that human transmission chains settle on what learners favour in this task, not that they reach the Bayesian prior, and it cannot tell sampling learners from MAP learners. | Active |
| [THEORY-493](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-493.md) | From core mereology, classical extensional mereology (GEM) is reached by exactly three pairings of a decomposition principle with an unrestricted-sum principle: Supplementation with Sum2, Strong Supplementation with Sum3, and Complementation with Sum1; Supplementation with Sum3, the pairing given by Simons (1987), does not yield it, because which definition of 'sum' is used decides which decomposition axiom is needed | Varzi, SEP "Mereology" (2003, revised June 2026), [LIT-124](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-124.md), read in full in [NOTE-163](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-163.md). A result the entry reports with citations (Hovda 2009; Cotnoir and Varzi 2019) and a countermodel (its Fig. 4; Pietruszczak 2000a, Pontow 2004), and which corrects Simons (1987), Casati and Varzi (1999) and the entry's own 2003 edition. The record has not checked the proofs. It is stated for first-order theories with a single primitive P and infinitary principles as axiom schemas, and it is a fact about axiom systems: it does not say classical mereology is true of anything. | Active |
| [THEORY-496](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-496.md) | In few-shot classification and multiple choice by language models up to 175B parameters, whether each demonstration's label is correct contributes little to the gain over zero-shot, while the distribution of the inputs, the label space and the paired format carry most of it | Min et al. (2022), [LIT-814](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-814.md), read in [NOTE-607](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-607.md). With k = 16 demonstrations, labels drawn at random from the correct label set cost 0–5 points against gold labels (2.6 on classification, 1.7 on multiple choice on average) across twelve model–inference combinations and 26 datasets. Out-of-distribution inputs, random English words as labels, or breaking the input–label pairing each cost far more. The random labels always come from the right label set, gaps reach about 14 points on single datasets, and the authors' reading that the models learn no new correspondence at test time is untested on tasks pretraining cannot have taught. | Active |
| [THEORY-498](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-498.md) | A mathematical structure whose domains are aspects of experience and whose axioms hold there is not thereby a structure of experience, because that test passes incompatible topologies on one set and every rescaling of a metric without consulting experience; requiring, for each relation, an aspect that changes exactly when a variation of experience breaks the relation removes those automatic passes, and has so far been met only by relative similarity and a visual topology, each on an assumed premise | Kleiner & Ludwig (2023; Synthese 2024), [LIT-143](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-143.md), read in full in [NOTE-135](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-135.md). The negative result is shown by construction: any set of aspects carries both the discrete topology and a coarser one, and a metric d passes whenever every C·d does. The replacement criterion (MSC) ties each relation to an aspect that co-varies with it under every variation. Its two positive cases rest on assumed transitivity and on the subsumptive unity thesis. The published version gives no structure that fails (MSC); the argument that metric spaces fail is in arXiv v1 only, and was withdrawn. | Active |
| [THEORY-501](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-501.md) | In weekly waste collection where each point's visit days are free and its bin capacity must cover the longest gap between visits, a genetic algorithm that searches visit schedules and derives bins from them builds routes about 6% cheaper than eight-hour Gurobi incumbents but buys about 20% more bin capacity, ending level on overall cost at its best of 30 runs and 4–6% worse on a typical run, on five 12-point instances where the incumbents' own optimality gaps are 26–32% | González et al. (2025), [LIT-008](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-008.md), read in [NOTE-015](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-015.md). The comparison is against incumbents whose distance from optimum is unknown, on five 12-point random subsets of one real instance, one of which was also used to tune the GA. Best of 30 against the MILP: −0.08% overall; against the MIQP: +1.70%; the GA's mean or median is +3.75% and +5.61%. The abstract's "able to match the results of exact solvers" says less than it appears to. On 40–163 points there is no bound or baseline. | Active |
| [THEORY-502](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-502.md) | Forman–Ricci curvature of a graph edge, taken with no cells above the edges, depends only on the weights of the edge, its two endpoints and the edges adjacent to it, and with unit weights reduces to 4 − deg(v₁) − deg(v₂); it is a local, closed-form degree-and-weight statistic that sees no triangles or cycles, unlike Ollivier's curvature, which needs a transport problem per edge | Weber, Saucan & Jost (2016; J. Complex Networks 2017), [LIT-020](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-020.md), read in full in [NOTE-026](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-026.md), which checked the formulas against page renders. The formula (Eq. 11) is Forman's (2003) Bochner–Weitzenböck curvature specialised to a 1-dimensional complex by dropping the parent terms; the unit-weight form is [NOTE-026](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-026.md)'s substitution, not stated in the paper. The paper's applications (an EMD distance between curvature distributions, a Ricci flow for change detection, a Laplacian flow for denoising) are one-table or one-figure demonstrations, and several of its formulas carry sign and consistency slips, so it is cited here for the definition only. | Active |
| [THEORY-503](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-503.md) | The nearest rank-r matrix to a real matrix in the least-squares norm keeps its r largest singular values and zeroes the rest; it is unique when the r-th and (r+1)-th singular values differ, its squared error is the sum of the dropped squares, and the singular-vector factors that build it are not unique | Eckart & Young (1936), [LIT-330](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-330.md), read in full in [NOTE-301](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-301.md), which checked the error bound. The argument is first-order stationarity on the orthogonal group plus two cited theorems (the SVD and a simultaneous-SVD criterion), and assumes a minimiser exists. Only the Frobenius norm and real matrices are covered. Uniqueness is of the approximating matrix, under a spectral gap, never of the factors; the paper's last section argues the canonic components cannot be read straightforwardly as psychological factors. | Active |
| [THEORY-504](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-504.md) | In the Gemma Scope sparse autoencoders on Gemma 2, the two fidelity measures disagree by site: residual-stream autoencoders cost more next-token loss than MLP or attention ones at comparable fraction of variance unexplained, and base-model autoencoders transfer to the instruction-tuned model by loss more than by variance explained | Lieberum et al. (2024), [LIT-611](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-611.md), read in [NOTE-482](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-482.md). Across every layer and sublayer of Gemma 2 2B and 9B, JumpReLU autoencoders on the residual stream raise the language model's loss more, when spliced in, than MLP and attention autoencoders whose FVU is about the same; and autoencoders trained on the base model lose little loss on instruction-tuned rollouts while showing a larger FVU gap. The authors' explanations (the residual stream is the bottleneck; fine-tuning re-weights old features) are conjectures, and the authors say no agreed metric of autoencoder quality exists. | Active |
| [THEORY-505](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-505.md) | Questionnaire items written for morality-as-cooperation's seven domains form seven factors when rated for relevance to moral decisions, in the UK, the US and Turkey, but not when rated as agreement with moral statements, and the two formats cannot be pooled into seven domains | Curry, Jones Chesters & Van Lissa (2019), [LIT-496](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-496.md), read in [NOTE-412](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-412.md), and the independent Turkish validation by Yilmaz, Harma & Doğruyol (2021), [LIT-513](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-513.md) ([NOTE-397](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-397.md)). Relevance items fit seven factors in all three samples (CFI .98 UK, .95 Turkey). Judgement items do not (CFI .87, .83), and a seven-domain model of both fails (CFI .73, .75). The items were written from the theory and selected for fit within each domain, several subscales correlate above .8, and no item is non-cooperative. This is evidence about the instrument's structure, not about what morality contains. | Active |
| [THEORY-508](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-508.md) | The Belousov–Zhabotinsky oscillation is a relaxation cycle in which autocatalytic production of HBrO₂ oxidizes the catalyst until bromide, released as the oxidized catalyst is reduced by bromomalonic acid, switches the autocatalysis off; a closed batch oscillates only as a transient of up to several thousand cycles on its way to equilibrium, and only a continuous-flow reactor sustains it indefinitely | Zhabotinsky (2007), [LIT-531](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-531.md), the Scholarpedia review by one of the reaction's eponyms, read in full in [NOTE-414](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-414.md). The mechanism is supported by the primary kinetics and by phase-resetting with injected Br⁻, Ag⁺ and Ce⁴⁺. The closed/open distinction matters for any use of BZ as a dissipative structure: a closed batch is a long transient, and only a fed reactor holds it away from equilibrium. The Oregonator models oscillation and excitability qualitatively, not quantitatively. The "several thousand cycles" figure is uncited, and the primary papers were not read. | Active |
